links.mechanism: With the Azores high weak, Atlantic depressions run south into Iberia and the western Mediterranean one after another, so winters tend to be wet, sometimes with flooding in Portugal, Spain and Morocco.
links.caveat: A wet winter needs the storms to actually arrive; a negative winter dominated by a stationary block can leave Iberia dry and cold instead.
links.evidence_note: The winter of 2009–10 brought the wettest season in decades to southern Iberia, with flooding in Andalusia and Portugal, the textbook negative-phase footprint.

links.mechanism: A weak Icelandic low and a blocking high over Greenland steer Arctic air south into the eastern United States, and coastal storms running up against the cold air tend to bring heavy snow to the big eastern cities.
links.caveat: The Pacific often has more say: whether a negative winter is snowy or merely cold depends on the moisture that El Niño or La Niña sends across the continent.
links.evidence_note: The record snows of February 2010 in Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia came in a winter that combined a strongly negative NAO with an El Niño; studies credit the NAO for the cold and El Niño for the moisture.

links.mechanism: With the Icelandic low weak and a high sitting near Greenland, mild air is drawn north over the Labrador Sea and west Greenland, so winters there tend to be much milder than usual.
links.caveat: The warmth is largest over west Greenland and Baffin Bay; the east coast, facing the Greenland Sea, shows less of it.

links.mechanism: Storms that cross a wet Mediterranean tend to continue east and bring more rain and snow to Turkey and the headwaters of the Tigris and Euphrates.
links.caveat: The connection is weaker and less steady than in Iberia and some studies do not find it at all; a wet winter here can just as well come from a local Mediterranean low.

links.mechanism: El Niño weakens the east-west overturning of air along the equator, so sinking, dry air settles over Indonesia and the winds along the equatorial Indian Ocean turn toward the west. Those winds push warm surface water away from Sumatra and let cooler water rise there, which is the start of a positive dipole.
links.caveat: The dipole has its own dynamics and can grow without El Niño, as in 1961, 1994 and 2019, and many El Niño years pass without one; whether it develops also depends on the state of the Indian Ocean in spring.
links.evidence_note: Strong positive dipoles fell in the El Niño years 1972, 1982, 1997, 2006 and 2015, and statistical studies find that El Niño accounts for a large share of dipole variability. How much of the rest is independent is still argued; the 2019 event, with no El Niño, is the standard counter-example.

links.mechanism: La Niña strengthens the rising air over Indonesia and turns the winds along the equatorial Indian Ocean toward the east, which piles warm water up against Sumatra and tends to tip the Indian Ocean into a negative dipole.
links.caveat: Negative dipoles are rarer and weaker than positive ones, and the pairing with La Niña is looser than the El Niño pairing; a La Niña year can pass with a neutral or even a positive dipole.
links.evidence_note: Negative dipoles fell in the La Niña years 1964, 1974, 1975, 1989, 1998 and 2010, but the relationship is not a mirror image of the El Niño one: the pathway between the two oceans is asymmetric and the negative side of it is less consistent.

links.mechanism: A negative dipole strengthens the rain over the eastern Indian Ocean and Indonesia in autumn; when it collapses in winter the winds over the western Pacific swing to westerly, which can start the warming that grows into an El Niño by the following year.
links.caveat: The Pacific has its own two-to-seven-year rhythm, and several studies find the Indian Ocean adds little once that rhythm is allowed for; a negative dipole in autumn is at most one of several nudges toward an El Niño a year later.
links.evidence_note: The link was proposed from the 1981-2009 record, where a negative dipole preceded most El Niño onsets by about fourteen months, and argued to hold across earlier decades. Others find the same statistics can be explained by the Pacific's own cycle, with the dipole tagging along rather than leading.

links.mechanism: A positive dipole weakens the rain over Indonesia in autumn; when it collapses in winter the winds over the western Pacific swing to easterly, which can start the cooling that grows into a La Niña by the following year.
links.caveat: Positive dipoles usually come with an El Niño, and an El Niño is often followed by a La Niña anyway, so it is hard to tell how much the dipole itself contributes; the Pacific's own cycle may explain most of it.
links.evidence_note: Reported in the same studies as the negative-dipole link and less robust than it, because the positive dipole rarely occurs on its own.

links.mechanism: In an El Niño winter the storm track over the North Pacific shifts and strengthens, and planetary-scale waves carry that disturbance up into the stratosphere and across to the Atlantic, where late in winter it tends to weaken the Icelandic low and the Azores high: a negative NAO.
links.caveat: The signal is modest, appears mostly in late winter, and is easily hidden by the Atlantic's own week-to-week swings; the strongest El Niños of 1982-83 and 1997-98 did not produce it, and the relationship has come and gone over the twentieth century.
links.evidence_note: Reviews find a late-winter tendency toward a negative NAO in moderate El Niño winters, with the stratosphere as the likely route; model experiments reproduce it. Very strong events seem to behave differently, and some periods show no signal at all.

links.mechanism: In a La Niña winter the North Pacific storm track weakens and shifts, and the disturbance that reaches the Atlantic tends to strengthen the westerlies there rather than weaken them, leaning the winter toward a positive NAO.
links.caveat: The La Niña signal over the Atlantic is weaker and less consistent than the El Niño one, and different studies find it in different months or not at all; a La Niña winter can easily be a negative NAO winter, as 2010-11 was.
links.evidence_note: One study of the twentieth century found the La Niña signal over the North Atlantic clearer than the El Niño one; later reviews find the opposite. Shown as contested because the literature does not agree.

links.mechanism: El Niño strengthens and stretches the Pacific jet stream so that it crosses North America further north and stronger than usual. Mild Pacific air flows across the Prairies and the Arctic air that normally pools there is held back.
links.caveat: A single Arctic outbreak can still make headlines in an El Niño winter; the tendency is for the season as a whole to average milder, not for cold snaps to vanish.
links.evidence_note: Shabbar and Khandekar found the winter warming over western and central Canada in almost every El Niño since 1900, and it is among the strongest ENSO temperature signals outside the tropics.

links.mechanism: Rising air over the warm central Pacific to the south of Hawaii is balanced by sinking air over the islands, which suppresses showers, while the storms of the north Pacific tend to pass north of them.
links.caveat: Not every El Niño winter is dry, and rainfall on the islands varies enormously from one valley to the next, so a wet windward slope can sit beside a parched leeward one.
links.evidence_note: Chu found dry winters following most El Niño onsets since the 1950s, with the driest conditions in the second winter of a long event.

links.mechanism: The rising branch of the tropical circulation moves out into the Pacific, and the compensating sinking air settles over the northern Amazon and the Caribbean coast of South America, cutting off the deep clouds that bring the rain.
links.caveat: The southern Amazon often escapes or even turns wetter, and the size of the drought also depends on the Atlantic, which decides how far north the rain belt sits.
links.evidence_note: The Ropelewski and Halpert maps show northern South America as one of the most consistent dry regions in El Niño; the 1997–98 and 2015–16 events brought record low river levels and widespread forest fires in Roraima and the northeastern Amazon.

links.mechanism: A warm eastern Pacific strengthens the trade winds and the sinking air over the Caribbean and Central America, and the mid-summer break in the rains lengthens, so the rainy season delivers less than usual, above all on the Pacific side.
links.caveat: The Caribbean coast, fed by moist trade winds, often sees little change or even more rain, and a warm tropical Atlantic can cancel the Pacific's drying.
links.evidence_note: The dry-season signal is strongest in the late rainy season (August–October); Giannini and colleagues found the Caribbean turns wetter in the early rainy season of the following year, which is not shown here.

links.mechanism: El Niño strengthens the subtropical jet stream across northern Mexico and the southern United States, steering a steady supply of Pacific storms across the desert Southwest that would otherwise pass further north.
links.caveat: The tendency is strongest in strong events; weak and central-Pacific El Niños have brought ordinary or even dry winters to Arizona and New Mexico.

links.mechanism: The band of warm water and rising air where South Pacific cyclones are born shifts east and toward the equator in El Niño, so storms tend to form near Fiji, Samoa and the Cook Islands, and further east, rather than in the Coral Sea.
links.caveat: It is where cyclones form that changes most reliably; the total count for the whole South Pacific rises only a little, and any one island can still be missed in a busy season.

links.mechanism: In El Niño the warm water and rising air move away from northern Australia toward the central Pacific, taking the conditions cyclones need with them, so fewer form in the Australian region and the first one tends to arrive later.
links.caveat: Fewer does not mean none: Cyclone Tracy, the most destructive in Australia's history, struck Darwin during the El Niño summer of 1974–75, so a quiet season can still contain a bad storm.
links.evidence_note: Nicholls showed in the 1970s and 1980s that the coming season's cyclone count could be foretold from the Southern Oscillation, one of the first seasonal forecasts of its kind.

links.mechanism: Warm water and rising air spread east along the equator, so typhoons tend to form further southeast in the open Pacific. That gives them a longer track over warm water before they meet land or cold air, and more of them reach the highest intensities.
links.caveat: The number of typhoons in a season hardly changes with ENSO, only where they form and how long they live, and the Philippines and Japan can still be hit hard in any year.
links.evidence_note: Wang and Chan and Camargo and Sobel both find more long-lived, intense storms in El Niño years; the 2015 season, with an unusually large number of very intense typhoons, fits the pattern.

links.mechanism: Cool water and sinking air over the western Pacific in El Niño set up a persistent high-pressure area over the sea east of the Philippines. Its southwesterly winds pump warm, moist air onto the coast of southern China through the winter and spring.
links.caveat: The wet signal fades if the event ends early, and the following summer is far less predictable: the great Yangtze flood of 1998 followed an El Niño but many other post-El Niño summers were unremarkable.

links.mechanism: The Kiremt rains are part of the same summer rain belt as the Indian monsoon. El Niño weakens the rising air over that whole belt and shifts the tropical easterly jet that feeds moisture into the highlands, so the rains come late and fall short.
links.caveat: Roughly a third of El Niño summers have brought near-normal Kiremt rain, and the western highlands are affected less than the northeast and the Rift Valley.
links.evidence_note: Korecha and Barnston found the state of the Pacific to be the best single predictor of Kiremt rainfall; the failures of 1984, 1987 and 2015 all came with El Niño.

links.mechanism: El Niño strengthens the westerly and southwesterly winds over New Zealand in summer. They bring cooler air from the Southern Ocean, more rain to the west coast and drier weather to the north and east.
links.caveat: The temperature change is small, a fraction of a degree on average, and the rainfall signal reverses between the west and east coasts, so no single word describes a New Zealand El Niño summer.

links.mechanism: As an El Niño peaks and fades, the rain belt that had swung east toward the central Pacific leaves the western Pacific under sinking air and cooler-than-usual water, and the dry season in Micronesia turns severe and long.
links.caveat: The drought follows only strong events reliably; after a weak El Niño the dry season may be ordinary, and the islands nearest the equator are hit harder than the northern Marianas.
links.evidence_note: Guam, Palau and the Marshall Islands declared water emergencies in the early months of 1983, 1998 and 2016, each following a strong El Niño; this delayed signal is used for drought warnings across the region.

links.mechanism: La Niña weakens the Pacific jet and favours a ridge of high pressure over the eastern Pacific, downstream of which cold Arctic air is drawn south across the Prairies and the northern Plains more often.
links.caveat: The cold signal in La Niña is weaker and less consistent than the warm signal in El Niño, and some La Niña winters on the Prairies have been close to normal.

links.mechanism: With the central Pacific cool, the sinking air that dries Hawaii in El Niño is absent, and winter fronts and cut-off lows tend to reach the islands more often.
links.caveat: The wet tendency in La Niña is weaker than the dry tendency in El Niño, and the islands' rain depends heavily on a few large storms whose timing no seasonal pattern controls.

links.mechanism: Rising air concentrates over the warm western Pacific and South America, and the northern Amazon, Colombia and Venezuela tend to sit under more active rain clouds than usual.
links.caveat: The wet response is less regular than the El Niño drought, and much of the region's flooding depends on the Atlantic and on the strength of the local rainy season.
links.evidence_note: Colombia's floods of 2010–11, during a strong La Niña, were the country's costliest weather disaster and fit the pattern.

links.mechanism: A cool eastern Pacific weakens the sinking air over the Caribbean and Central America and shortens the mid-summer break in the rains, so the rainy season tends to deliver more, and Atlantic hurricanes, which La Niña also favours, add to it.
links.caveat: The extra rain can be modest, and whether it turns into floods depends on hurricane tracks that no seasonal tendency predicts.

links.mechanism: La Niña shifts the storm track north into the Pacific Northwest and weakens the subtropical jet, so Pacific storms rarely reach the Southwest and northern Mexico and the winter tends to be dry.
links.caveat: Dry winters have many origins, and a single slow-moving storm can rescue a La Niña season; the persistent Southwest drought of the early 2000s spanned La Niña and neutral years alike.

links.mechanism: In La Niña the warm water and rising air retreat west toward the Coral Sea, so cyclones tend to form near Australia and Vanuatu and seldom reach the islands east of Fiji.
links.caveat: Cyclones can still develop near Fiji and Tonga in La Niña years, and the eastern islands' counts are small enough that one storm changes the season's story.

links.mechanism: Warm water and the rising air of the Pacific rain belt sit close to northern Australia in La Niña, so more cyclones form in the region and the first one tends to arrive earlier in the season.
links.caveat: Cyclone numbers in the Australian region have fallen over recent decades for reasons that are still debated, so a La Niña season today may only match what an average season brought fifty years ago.

links.mechanism: Typhoons in La Niña tend to form further northwest, close to the Philippines and the South China Sea, and so have less time over warm water to strengthen before reaching land.
links.caveat: Forming closer to Asia can mean more landfalls even though storms are weaker on average, so a quieter season by this measure is not necessarily a safer one for the coast.

links.mechanism: A warm western Pacific in La Niña favours low pressure east of the Philippines, so the moist southwesterly feed onto southern China is replaced by dry northerly winter monsoon air.
links.caveat: The dry La Niña signal is weaker and less regular than the wet El Niño one, and cold northerly outbreaks can bring snow and freezing rain to the south, as in January 2008.

links.mechanism: A cool Pacific strengthens the rising air over Africa and South Asia and the tropical easterly jet that carries moisture to the Ethiopian highlands, so the Kiremt rains tend to be full.
links.caveat: Wetter summers bring their own harm, with floods along the Awash and in the lowlands, and the signal is weaker than the El Niño drought.

links.mechanism: La Niña brings more northeasterly winds over New Zealand in summer, carrying warm, humid air from the subtropics, so summers tend to be warmer, with more rain in the north and east.
links.caveat: Warm summers in New Zealand also come from warm seas around the country and from the Southern Annular Mode, so a La Niña is neither needed nor enough for one.
links.evidence_note: The record-warm summer of 2017–18 came with a weak La Niña and unusually warm seas around the country; both are usually credited with the record.

links.mechanism: A positive North Atlantic Oscillation means a strong pressure contrast between Iceland and the Azores. That contrast drives a fast jet stream aimed at the British Isles and the North Sea, and storm after storm rides along it.
links.caveat: A positive winter has more and stronger storms on average, but the most damaging single storm of a decade can still fall in an ordinary winter; the count changes, not the possibility.

links.mechanism: The strong westerlies of a positive winter carry mild Atlantic air over the Alps and leave high pressure sitting over them, so precipitation falls as rain rather than snow at low and middle altitudes and what snow there is melts sooner.
links.caveat: High-altitude resorts often do well in a positive winter, since the storms still bring moisture, and a single cold spell in a mild winter can lay down a season's worth of snow in the valleys.
links.evidence_note: Beniston tied the run of snow-poor Alpine winters in the late 1980s and 1990s to the strongly positive North Atlantic Oscillation of those years; later work finds the link clear below about 1,500 metres and weaker above.

links.mechanism: The strong westerlies of a positive winter carry mild, moist Atlantic air far inland across Scandinavia and European Russia toward the Urals and western Siberia, holding off the Siberian cold.
links.caveat: The mild tendency fades with distance east; in central Siberia and beyond other patterns matter more, and even a positive winter can contain a deep cold spell when the westerlies pause.

links.mechanism: In a negative winter the pressure contrast across the Atlantic weakens, the jet stream slows and wanders south, and northwest Europe often sits under a blocking high with calm, cold weather while the storms go to Iberia and the Mediterranean.
links.caveat: A quiet stormy season is not a calm winter: negative phases bring their own hazards, with cold spells, snow and freezing fog in place of wind.

links.mechanism: A negative winter lets cold continental air settle over the Alps and sends storms along a southern track that brings heavy snow to the southern and western Alps in particular, so snow tends to be deep and to last.
links.caveat: If the negative phase brings dry, blocked weather rather than southern storms, the winter can be cold but snow-poor, so the sign is less certain than the temperature signal.

links.mechanism: When the westerlies falter in a negative winter the Siberian high can extend west, and cold continental air spreads over European Russia instead of being pushed back by mild air from the Atlantic.
links.caveat: Russia's coldest winters often owe as much to a blocking high over the Urals, which the North Atlantic Oscillation does not control, so a negative phase raises the odds of cold without deciding it.
links.evidence_note: The winter of 2009–10, a record negative phase, was one of the coldest in Moscow for decades; the record-warm Russian summer that followed it had nothing to do with the North Atlantic Oscillation.

links.mechanism: With the westerly belt tightened toward the pole, the winter cold fronts that bring the southwest its rain pass to the south of the coast instead of crossing it.
links.caveat: The mode explains only part of the winter rainfall here, and it swings within weeks, so a winter that leans positive on average can still hold a few very wet fronts.
links.evidence_note: Daily and seasonal studies agree on the sign, with the mode explaining up to about fifteen percent of the week-to-week rainfall variance in winter, comparable with ENSO. The region's long decline in winter rain since the 1970s is only partly explained by the mode's trend.

links.mechanism: With the westerly belt loosened and spread toward the equator, more winter cold fronts reach the southwest coast and the rain they carry falls there.
links.caveat: A negative winter brings more fronts, not necessarily wetter ones; a dry winter is still possible if the fronts arrive weak, and the long-term decline in rain here continues under either phase.

links.mechanism: In winter the southern coast, Victoria and Tasmania get their rain from westerly fronts; with the belt held to the south, fewer fronts cross the coast.
links.caveat: The Indian Ocean Dipole and ENSO act on the same region in the same months and can outweigh the mode; and the same positive phase tends to bring the east coast more rain once summer comes.
links.evidence_note: Found in daily rainfall for southern Victoria, South Australia and western Tasmania, and in seasonal totals; the winter signal is the most consistent of the mode's Australian effects.

links.mechanism: With the westerly belt spread north, more winter fronts cross the southern coast, Victoria and Tasmania and bring their rain with them.
links.caveat: A positive dipole or an El Niño in the same year tends to dry the same region and can cancel this; in spring the negative phase turns hot and dry over the east instead.

links.mechanism: In summer the positive phase brings more onshore easterly winds to the southern east coast, feeding moist air into New South Wales and cooling the hot inland, so summer rain tends to increase there.
links.caveat: The summer signal is weaker than the winter one, sits on the coast rather than inland, and can be swamped by ENSO; western Tasmania tends to dry at the same time.
links.evidence_note: Reported for daily rainfall on the southern east coast, with lower maximum temperatures over most of subtropical eastern Australia; the mode's summer footprint has shifted over the decades.

links.mechanism: In spring and summer the negative phase weakens the onshore easterlies and lets hot, dry northwesterly winds from the interior cross eastern Australia, raising temperatures and fire danger and cutting rain.
links.caveat: Weeks of negative mode, not a season of it, drive most of the damage, and a wet La Niña can override the tendency; the strongest cases came after rare weakenings of the stratospheric polar vortex.
links.evidence_note: The spring of 2019, the most strongly negative on record, brought record heat and drought to subtropical eastern Australia ahead of the Black Summer fires; hot, dry springs have followed earlier vortex weakenings too.

links.mechanism: In summer the positive phase weakens the westerlies over New Zealand as the belt contracts to the south; with less wind off the Southern Ocean the country tends to be warmer, and the western hills drier.
links.caveat: The effect is a summer one; in winter the mode's footprint over New Zealand is patchy, and ENSO's own summer wind pattern can pull the other way.
links.evidence_note: Station temperatures and rainfall follow the mode's summer wind change closely; the south of the country warms most, and the west coast dries.

links.mechanism: In summer the negative phase strengthens the westerlies over New Zealand as the belt spreads north, bringing more cool Southern Ocean air and more rain to the western hills.
links.caveat: A warm La Niña summer can override the cooling, and the effect is on the summer average, not on any one week.

links.mechanism: The westerlies that water southern Chile tighten toward the pole and strengthen over the ocean, so fewer fronts and less rain reach the coast south of 40°S, and the region warms.
links.caveat: The drying is clearest in the annual mean and on the windward Chilean side; ENSO adds its own swings in central Chile, further north, which can look like the mode's.
links.evidence_note: Station records across southern South America show the drying and warming consistently, and the long-term warming of Patagonia has been traced to the mode's trend.

links.mechanism: With the westerly belt loosened, more fronts reach the Chilean coast south of 40°S and rainfall on the windward side of the Andes tends to increase.
links.caveat: The Argentine side sits in the rain shadow and gains little; and a negative season is rarer than a positive one nowadays.

links.mechanism: Stronger summer westerlies push more air over the peninsula's mountain spine; it descends on the eastern side as a warm foehn wind, so the northeast of the peninsula warms sharply.
links.caveat: The warming is three times larger on the eastern side than the western, and weak south of about 65°S; the western stations respond more to the sea ice and the ocean.
links.evidence_note: The summer warming of the northeastern peninsula since the 1960s, and the loss of the northern Larsen ice shelves, are tied to the mode's summer trend; the relationship has shifted between decades.

links.mechanism: Weaker summer westerlies mean less air is forced over the peninsula and fewer warm foehn winds on its eastern side, so the summer tends to be cooler.
links.caveat: The cooling is a tendency of the summer average on the northeastern coast; a single warm spell can still set records if the mode swings back for a week.

links.mechanism: With the storm track and the South Atlantic high shifted south, fewer winter cold fronts reach the Cape and the moisture that feeds them passes to the south.
links.caveat: Studies of the whole of South Africa, most of which has summer rain, find the opposite sign for the country as a whole; this link is for the winter-rainfall corner around Cape Town only.
links.evidence_note: Six of the eight driest winters between 1948 and 2004 came with a positive mode, and the 2015–2017 "Day Zero" drought came with a poleward shift of the storm track and a positive mode; a hemisphere-wide station study finds wetter conditions over much of South Africa, so the sign depends on which part of the country is meant.

links.mechanism: With the storm track spread north, more winter cold fronts reach the Cape, fed by moisture off the South Atlantic, and the winter tends to be wetter.
links.caveat: Six of the seven wettest winters since 1948 came with a negative mode, but the sample is small and the mode flips within weeks, so the season average may hide a dry spell.

links.mechanism: In spring the positive phase sets up a high-pressure anomaly over southern South America and the adjacent Atlantic that weakens the flow of moist air into Uruguay, southern Brazil and northeast Argentina.
links.caveat: The sign of this link changed between the 1960s–70s and the 1980s–90s, and in winter it runs the other way; ENSO's spring effect on the same region is stronger and the mode mostly modulates it.
links.evidence_note: Reported for spring from the 1980s onward; in the earlier decades the same phase brought more rain, so the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: In spring the negative phase favours a low-pressure anomaly over southern South America that draws moist air into Uruguay, southern Brazil and northeast Argentina.
links.caveat: Reported for recent decades only, with the opposite sign before the 1980s; La Niña tends to dry the same region in the same season and can override it.

links.mechanism: El Niño warms the tropics and shifts the winds of the subtropics, which changes how weather systems are steered in the Southern Hemisphere and tends to weaken and spread the westerly belt in the austral summer: a negative mode.
links.caveat: Roughly a quarter of the summer mode follows ENSO; the rest is the atmosphere's own noise, and the pairing has been strong in some decades and weak in others.
links.evidence_note: Found for the austral summer in the reanalysis record, and in the 1990s in spring as well; in the 1980s the two patterns interfered rather than lining up, so the link is shown as probable rather than established.

links.mechanism: La Niña cools the tropics and strengthens the subtropical winds, which tends to tighten the westerly belt toward the pole in the austral summer: a positive mode.
links.caveat: The same quarter-share applies: most of the summer mode is not set by ENSO, and a La Niña summer can still lean negative for weeks.
links.evidence_note: The same summer relationship as the El Niño link, read the other way; when the two line up, a wet La Niña summer on the east coast of Australia gets the mode's onshore winds on top.

links.mechanism: Warm water in the Gulf of Alaska and a deep Aleutian low pump mild Pacific air north over Alaska through the winter.
links.caveat: The oscillation is a decade-scale average; any one winter inside a positive phase can be cold if the Aleutian low sits in the wrong place for a few weeks, and much of the signal is El Niño's own winter pattern.
links.evidence_note: The warm-phase regression shows Alaska and northwest North America warm in winter, and Alaska's climate stepped warmer at the 1976–77 flip; the mixed causes of the oscillation mean the tendency is rated probable rather than established.

links.mechanism: Cool water in the Gulf of Alaska and a weak Aleutian low leave Alaska under its own cold air through the winter.
links.caveat: A single winter inside a negative phase can still be mild; the tendency is over the decade, and a strong El Niño can override it.

links.mechanism: Warm coastal water and a deep Aleutian low steer mild Pacific air onto the Northwest coast and shift the storms away from it, so winters tend to be milder and drier, with less mountain snow.
links.caveat: ENSO acts on the same region in the same months and its swings are larger; inside a positive phase a La Niña winter can still be cold and snowy.
links.evidence_note: The warm-phase regression shows northwest North America warm and the Pacific Northwest dry in winter; the 2014–15 winter, after the 2014 swing to positive, brought record-low snowpack to Oregon and Washington with near-normal precipitation falling as rain.

links.mechanism: Cool coastal water and a weak Aleutian low leave the Northwest coast under cooler air with the storm track on top of it, so winters tend to be cooler and wetter, with more mountain snow.
links.caveat: An El Niño winter inside a negative phase can still be mild and dry; ENSO's signal is the larger one.

links.mechanism: The deep Aleutian low of the warm phase sets up a ridge over western Canada that carries mild Pacific air across the Rockies onto the Prairies in winter.
links.caveat: This is El Niño's winter pattern held on average for a decade, and it is weaker than El Niño's own; a cold winter is still possible inside a positive phase.
links.evidence_note: Northwest North America, including western Canada, is warm in the warm-phase winter regression; El Niño's own effects over North America are stronger and steadier in the warm phase of the North Pacific.

links.mechanism: With a weak Aleutian low and no ridge over western Canada, Arctic air sits over the Prairies more often in winter.
links.caveat: Weaker than La Niña's own cold tendency here and easily overridden by an El Niño winter inside the phase.

links.mechanism: The deep Aleutian low of the warm phase strengthens the subtropical jet across the southern United States in winter and steers Pacific storms into the Southwest and northern Mexico.
links.caveat: Rainfall signals of the oscillation are weaker and patchier than the temperature ones, and the 2014–15 winter of a freshly positive phase left California in drought.
links.evidence_note: The warm-phase regression shows the Southwest and northern Mexico wet in winter, and multidecadal droughts in the United States cluster in the cool phase; but the precipitation signal is weak and El Niño does most of the work, so the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: With a weak Aleutian low the subtropical jet is weak and the winter storms stay north of the Southwest, so winters tend to be drier.
links.caveat: Weak in any one year; the droughts of the 1950s and of 1999–2002 fell in the cool phase, but a single El Niño winter inside it can be very wet.
links.evidence_note: Half of the multidecadal variation in drought frequency over the United States is tied to the Pacific and Atlantic oscillations together, with the cool Pacific phase favouring drought; the link is shown as contested because the year-to-year signal is small.

links.mechanism: El Niño deepens the Aleutian low through the "atmospheric bridge", which cools the central North Pacific and warms the water along the North American coast, the pattern of a positive oscillation; the ocean then remembers it from one winter to the next.
links.caveat: The oscillation also has its own North Pacific sources and a decade-long memory, so a single El Niño tips the index for a season or a year rather than flipping the phase; the 1997–98 El Niño was followed by a cool phase, not a warm one.
links.evidence_note: A simple model of ENSO forcing plus the re-emergence of last winter's anomalies plus noise reproduces the index well, and the current view is that the oscillation is a mix of processes rather than one, with the tropics supplying much of it.

links.mechanism: La Niña weakens the Aleutian low through the same bridge, which warms the central North Pacific and cools the coastal water, the pattern of a negative oscillation.
links.caveat: One La Niña nudges the index; the phase itself turns on the ocean's decade-long memory, so a La Niña inside a warm phase does not end it.
links.evidence_note: The same bridge as the El Niño link, read the other way; the run of La Niña years around 1999–2001 and 2010–12 fell in a mostly cool phase, but the fit is loose year by year.

links.mechanism: A warm tropical North Atlantic feeds storms more energy and comes with weaker wind shear over the main hurricane-forming region between Africa and the Caribbean, so more storms form and more of them grow into major hurricanes.
links.caveat: El Niño can quieten a season inside a warm phase, and a single season's count swings widely for reasons of its own; the tendency is over the decades.
links.evidence_note: Activity from 1995 on roughly doubled that of 1971–1994, with a two-and-a-half-fold rise in major hurricanes, and the same warm-Atlantic, low-shear pairing marks the active decades before 1970; a long climate-model run reproduces the association.

links.mechanism: A cool tropical North Atlantic and stronger wind shear over the hurricane-forming region between Africa and the Caribbean tend to tear developing storms apart, so seasons are quieter.
links.caveat: A quiet phase still produces destructive hurricanes (Andrew in 1992 fell in one), and a La Niña can make a season inside a cool phase busy.

links.mechanism: A warm North Atlantic, warmer than the ocean south of the equator, pulls the tropical rain belt north in summer and draws moist air further inland over West Africa, so the Sahel's short rainy season tends to be stronger.
links.caveat: The Sahel also answers the Pacific and the Indian Ocean, and a warm phase does not guarantee a wet year; the tendency is over decades, with wet and dry years inside each phase.
links.evidence_note: The wet Sahel of the 1950s and the drought of the 1970s and 1980s line up with the warm and cool Atlantic phases, model runs driven by the observed sea temperatures reproduce the swing, and a 1400-year climate-model run shows the same link. What set the Atlantic's phases is argued over: pollution haze and volcanic dust may have driven much of the twentieth-century cooling. The link from the ocean to the rain holds either way.

links.mechanism: A cool North Atlantic, cool relative to the ocean south of the equator, holds the tropical rain belt further south in summer, so the Sahel's rains tend to fail.
links.caveat: The tendency is over decades: even in the drought decades a few summers were wet, and the drying of the 1970s and 1980s was helped along by warm water in the Indian Ocean and the tropics generally.
links.evidence_note: The Sahel drought of the 1970s and 1980s coincided with the cool phase from the mid-1960s to 1994, and the drying trend is reproduced by models driven with the observed sea temperatures.

links.mechanism: With a warm North Atlantic, high pressure over the ocean and the Gulf of Mexico sends less moisture north onto the Plains in summer, so the growing season tends to run dry.
links.caveat: The Pacific matters at least as much: the worst multidecadal droughts came when the Atlantic was warm and the Pacific cool at the same time, and any one summer can be wet inside a warm phase.
links.evidence_note: During warm phases most of the United States sees less rain than usual, mainly in summer, including the Midwest droughts of the 1930s and 1950s; about half of the multidecadal swing in drought over the United States is tied to the Atlantic and Pacific oscillations together.

links.mechanism: With a cool North Atlantic the summer flow of moisture out of the Gulf of Mexico onto the Plains tends to be stronger, so summers run wetter.
links.caveat: A cool phase does not rule out drought: the Pacific can dry the Plains on its own, and single summers vary widely.
links.evidence_note: The wet periods of the Great Plains in the twentieth century fell in cool-Atlantic decades, and river flows in the central United States run higher between warm phases.

links.mechanism: A warm North Atlantic warms the air arriving over western Europe in summer and shifts the summer weather pattern so that the continent runs warmer, with more rain in the north-west and less in the south.
links.caveat: The effect is a few tenths of a degree over a decade; any one summer is set far more by the weather of that summer, and the warming trend from greenhouse gases now runs alongside it.
links.evidence_note: Observations and model experiments tie the multidecadal swings in summer climate over western Europe to basin-wide changes in the Atlantic, and the shift to warmer summers in the mid-1990s is attributed largely to the ocean's swing to warm.

links.mechanism: A cool North Atlantic cools the air arriving over western Europe in summer, so summers tend to run cooler.
links.caveat: Small against the year-to-year swings of summer weather and against the warming trend; the cool summers of the 1960s to 1980s are the example, and other things lay behind them as well.

links.mechanism: When the North Atlantic is warmer than the South Atlantic the tropical rain belt sits further north in the early months of the year and reaches the Nordeste less, so its short rainy season tends to be weaker.
links.caveat: What matters for the Nordeste is the north–south contrast across the tropical Atlantic in that particular spring, and the Pacific; the slow basin-wide warming is only one part of that contrast, so the link is shown as contested.
links.evidence_note: Drier Nordeste seasons in warm phases appear in observations and in a long climate-model run, but the instrumental record holds only a few phases, and forecasts of Nordeste rain lean on the year's own Atlantic contrast and on ENSO.

links.mechanism: When the North Atlantic is cooler than the South Atlantic the tropical rain belt reaches further south in the early months of the year, so the Nordeste's rainy season tends to be stronger.
links.caveat: One part of the year's Atlantic contrast, and easily overridden by an El Niño; shown as contested.

links.mechanism: A warm North Atlantic is proposed to warm the air over Eurasia in late summer, which keeps the land–sea temperature contrast that drives the monsoon going for longer, so the monsoon tends to be a little stronger and to withdraw later.
links.caveat: Mostly a model result about a small multidecadal tilt; ENSO and the Indian Ocean set any one monsoon, and studies disagree on how much the Atlantic adds.
links.evidence_note: Statistical work links the multidecadal swings of Indian and Sahel rain and of hurricanes to the Atlantic, and one model traces a pathway through the temperature of the upper air over Eurasia; the signal is small and the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: A cool North Atlantic is proposed to cool the air over Eurasia in late summer, weakening the contrast that drives the monsoon, so it tends to withdraw earlier and deliver a little less rain.
links.caveat: Mostly a model result; small against ENSO and the Indian Ocean, and shown as contested.

links.mechanism: A warm North Atlantic warms and moistens the lower atmosphere over the ocean in winter, which is proposed to weaken the Icelandic low and the Azores high, the negative side of the NAO, partly by way of the stratosphere.
links.caveat: The NAO swings within weeks under its own weather, and the Atlantic's tilt is small and slow; it shows up in decade averages and in model experiments, not reliably in any one winter, so the link is shown as contested.
links.evidence_note: Model experiments forced with a warm North Atlantic produce a negative-NAO-like winter circulation, and the decadal record leans the same way, but the response depends on how the model treats the stratosphere and the observed record holds only a few phases.

links.mechanism: A cool North Atlantic is proposed to sharpen the winter contrast between the Icelandic low and the Azores high, the positive side of the NAO.
links.caveat: A small, slow tilt against the NAO's own swings, seen in decade averages and model experiments; shown as contested.
links.evidence_note: The composite and model results for the warm phase imply the reverse for the cool one; the positive-NAO winters of the late 1980s and early 1990s fell in a cool Atlantic phase.

links.mechanism: Warm water in the Gulf of Guinea feeds the rain clouds over the coast directly and holds the tropical rain belt at the coast through its main rainy season, so the coast tends to be wetter.
links.caveat: The coast's rains also depend on when the rain belt jumps north to the Sahel; a weak or late event adds little, and a single wet month can come from the weather alone.
links.evidence_note: Wet years on the Guinea coast come with a weaker-than-usual cold tongue in early summer, the leading pattern of tropical Atlantic sea-temperature variability is coupled to rain on the Gulf of Guinea coast, and the review of the mode names the coast as its clearest rainfall footprint.

links.mechanism: A strong cold tongue off the Gulf of Guinea cools the air over the coast, starves the rain clouds and lets the rain belt leave the coast early, so the coast's rainy season tends to be weaker.
links.caveat: A single season can still be wet if the rain belt lingers; the tendency is clearest in strong events.

links.mechanism: Warm water in the Gulf of Guinea holds the rain belt at the coast and keeps it from moving as far north as usual, so the Sahel tends to get less rain in a warm summer.
links.caveat: This coast–Sahel see-saw was clear before the 1970s and then nearly vanished: since then the Pacific and Indian Oceans have pulled the Sahel the other way in the same summers, and a warm Atlantic summer has often come with a wet Sahel.
links.evidence_note: Models forced with a warm equatorial Atlantic shift the rain belt toward the coast and dry the Sahel, and the pattern is in the older observations; but the see-saw broke down after the 1970s as the Sahel came to follow the whole tropics rather than the Atlantic alone, so the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: A strong cold tongue in the Gulf of Guinea pushes the rain belt off the coast and further north than usual in summer, so the Sahel tends to get more rain.
links.caveat: Clear only in the older record; since the 1970s the Sahel has followed the Pacific and the Indian Ocean more than the Atlantic, and the see-saw with the coast has faded.

links.mechanism: Rain clouds rising over a warm equatorial Atlantic set up a wave in the upper air that reaches around the globe and sinks over India, which is proposed to hold back the monsoon a little.
links.caveat: A small effect next to ENSO's, found mainly in models and in the part of the monsoon record that ENSO does not explain; not every warm Atlantic summer brings a weak monsoon.
links.evidence_note: The part of Indian monsoon rainfall not tied to ENSO correlates with south equatorial Atlantic sea temperature in observations and model ensembles, and a simple wave mechanism reproduces the teleconnection; the signal is small and the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: Rain rising over a warm equatorial Atlantic in summer strengthens the east–west overturning of the tropical air, with air sinking over the central Pacific; the stronger trade winds there lift the cool water in the east and start the Pacific toward a La Niña by the following winter.
links.caveat: Seen since the late 1960s and not before, and a nudge rather than a trigger: the Pacific has its own timing, and a warm Atlantic summer inside a developing El Niño does not stop it.
links.evidence_note: Since the late 1960s summer Atlantic Niños have favoured following-winter Pacific La Niñas, and Atlantic Niñas Pacific El Niños, in the observations and in model runs where only the Atlantic is set from observations; the reverse link, from the Pacific to the Atlantic, is weak and inconsistent.

links.mechanism: A cold equatorial Atlantic in summer weakens the rain rising over it, which loosens the trade winds over the central Pacific and lets warm water spread east, starting the Pacific toward an El Niño by the following winter.
links.caveat: Seen since the late 1960s and not before; a nudge to the Pacific's own timing, not a trigger.
links.evidence_note: The same study that found Atlantic Niños ahead of Pacific La Niñas found Atlantic Niñas ahead of Pacific El Niños over the same decades, with the same mechanism in reverse.

links.mechanism: Rain rising over the warm Indian Ocean warms the air high above the tropics, and that warmth spreads east as a wave along the equator. Over the western Pacific it dries the air and builds a strong high-pressure area, whose winds pump moist air up the Yangtze valley and hold the summer rain front there.
links.caveat: The strength of the high, not just whether there was an El Niño the winter before, decides how heavy the rains are; a weak or short-lived basin warming adds little, and the front's position in any one week is weather.
links.evidence_note: The summer after an El Niño brings a warm tropical Indian Ocean, an anomalous high over the subtropical northwest Pacific and heavier Meiyu–Baiu rain over East Asia; model runs with only the Indian Ocean warming reproduce the high, and the review of the mechanism treats the basin warming as the memory that carries the pattern into summer.

links.mechanism: A cool Indian Ocean gives less rain and a cooler upper air over the tropics, so the western Pacific high stays weak and sits further east, and less moist air is pumped up the Yangtze valley in summer.
links.caveat: The cooling after a La Niña is weaker and shorter than the warming after an El Niño, so the dry tendency is less reliable than the wet one; shown one tier lower for that reason.
links.evidence_note: Statistical studies that regress the Asian summer monsoon on the basin-mode index find the wet and dry signs together; the physical work is mostly on the warm phase, and El Niño and La Niña differ in how strongly they reach the Indian Ocean.

links.mechanism: The warm air spreading east from the Indian Ocean dries the western Pacific and sets up a high-pressure area over the Philippine Sea, with sinking air and stronger wind shear where typhoons usually form, so fewer of them form in the summer after an El Niño.
links.caveat: Clearest after strong El Niños, and the effect is on the number of storms over the open Pacific: the South China Sea can be busier at the same time, and any one typhoon can still strike.
links.evidence_note: In the summer following a strong El Niño typhoon numbers fall over the northwest Pacific despite little change in the local sea temperature, and the analysis traces the fall to the El Niño-induced Indian Ocean warming through the high and the shear it sets up.

links.mechanism: A cool Indian Ocean leaves the western Pacific high weak, with more rising air and weaker wind shear over the Philippine Sea, which is proposed to allow a busier typhoon season.
links.caveat: Studied mainly for the warm phase after strong El Niños; the cool phase is weaker and the reverse effect is an inference from the mechanism rather than a well-tested result.
links.evidence_note: The typhoon study covers summers after strong El Niños only; the reverse is drawn as contested because the physical argument runs both ways but the cool-phase evidence is thin.

links.mechanism: The high-pressure area over the Philippine Sea that the warm basin sustains carries warm, moist air onto the coast of southern China through spring and into early summer, keeping the rainy season wet.
links.caveat: In spring this arrow overlaps El Niño's own wet signal on the same coast, and much of what it shows is the tail of that; a weak basin warming adds little once the El Niño has faded.
links.evidence_note: Model runs with the basin warming alone reproduce the anticyclone over the Philippine and South China Seas and more rain along the East Asian front through spring, and the observational analysis of the mode finds the same anticyclone in early summer.

links.mechanism: With a cool basin the high over the Philippine Sea is weak or absent, so less moist air is carried onto the coast of southern China in spring and early summer.
links.caveat: The tail of a La Niña's own dry signal covers the same months; the cool phase is the weaker of the two.
links.evidence_note: The regression studies find both signs; the model work is on the warm phase.

links.mechanism: A warm Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal give up more moisture to the monsoon winds, which carry it onto the subcontinent, so the summer rains tend to be heavier once the monsoon is under way.
links.caveat: The studies disagree: one finds the onset delayed by about a week when the basin is warm, others find heavier rain through the season, and the warm basin usually arrives as an El Niño is fading into a La Niña, which favours a good monsoon on its own. Shown as contested for that reason; the card says so.
links.evidence_note: The observational analysis of the basin mode finds the southwest monsoon strengthened over the Arabian Sea, and the covariance study finds more South Asian summer rain with a warm basin, while the model study with the December–May warming finds the onset delayed by six to seven days; the sign and the size are both open.

links.mechanism: In the spring after an El Niño the air over the North Indian Ocean sinks more and the winds aloft shear more, and the monsoon's arrival tends to be late, which is proposed to leave fewer of the storms that form in the weeks before the monsoon.
links.caveat: The least certain arrow from this driver: reliable storm counts begin with the satellite era, the studies are few, none of them isolates the basin itself, and the Bay of Bengal's spring storms are admitted to be unexplained on so small a sample. The cyclone that struck Gujarat in June 1998, a warm-basin year, is the standing warning.
links.evidence_note: Bay of Bengal storm activity is negatively correlated with the Pacific's El Niño index at a lead of about five months, which is the season the basin is warm; Arabian Sea storms in May and June go with an early and a late monsoon onset respectively; but the study of the whole basin says the causes of April–June variability have yet to be found, so the link is shown as contested.

links.mechanism: Rain rising over the warm Indian Ocean drives an easterly wind over Indonesia and the far western Pacific. That wind pushes warm surface water west and sends a wave of cooler water east along the equator, which ends the El Niño quickly and tips the Pacific toward La Niña by the summer.
links.caveat: Works mostly after strong El Niños, and the Pacific has its own timing: some El Niños fade without a La Niña following, and the basin's push is one of several reasons an El Niño ends.
links.evidence_note: Indian Ocean warming produces the easterly wind over the western Pacific in the mature phase of El Niño, which helps its rapid termination and a fast transition to La Niña, mostly for relatively strong El Niños and typically a year after the peak; models show the Indian Ocean is the main source of that wind.

links.mechanism: El Niño shifts the tropical rain east and puts sinking, clear air over the Indian Ocean, with weaker winds; more sunshine and less evaporation let the whole basin gather heat through the winter, and a slow wave in the ocean south of the equator keeps the warmth into the following summer.
links.caveat: The warming trails the El Niño by about a season and is strongest when a positive Indian Ocean Dipole falls in the same year; a weak El Niño may warm the basin only a little.
links.evidence_note: The Indian Ocean warms basin-wide during El Niño with a lag of one season through the atmospheric bridge, sustained by surface heat fluxes and, when a dipole coincides, by ocean waves in the west; the north Indian Ocean's second warming peak persists through the summer.

links.mechanism: La Niña pulls the tropical rain west, so more cloud and stronger winds sit over the Indian Ocean, which cools the basin through the winter after a La Niña begins.
links.caveat: The cooling is weaker and shorter than the warming after an El Niño: the tropical rain answers a cold Pacific less strongly than a warm one, which is also why La Niñas tend to linger.
links.evidence_note: The bridge works in both directions in the observations, but El Niño and La Niña are not mirror images: the atmosphere's response to a cold Pacific is weaker, which the asymmetry study links to the different durations of the two.

links.mechanism: A warm northern tropical Atlantic with the rain belt sitting north puts warm water, moist air and weak wind shear over the sea where hurricanes are born, and shifts the birthplace of storms toward the open Atlantic, where they have room to grow.
links.caveat: The mode peaks in spring and the hurricane season runs from June; in some years the spring contrast has faded by then. An El Niño in the same year works the other way and the two can cancel, which is what the map shows when both are in play.
links.evidence_note: The mode is strongly related to seasonal hurricane activity on year-to-year and decadal time scales, through local conditions that all cooperate; a large part of overall activity is explained by shifts in where storms form, which track the mode; in summer the mode keeps its spring structure and reduces the wind shear over the tropical Atlantic, which model runs reproduce.

links.mechanism: A cool northern tropical Atlantic with the rain belt sitting south leaves cooler water, drier air and stronger wind shear over the hurricane breeding grounds, and storms that do form start closer to Africa's coast and the Caribbean, with less room to grow.
links.caveat: A La Niña in the same year favours storms and can offset the quiet tendency; the relation is with the season as a whole, and a single strong storm can still form.
links.evidence_note: The negative phase, with cool northern and warm southern tropical Atlantic water, inhibits Atlantic storms on its own, and the framework relating the mode to hurricane activity holds in both signs on interannual and multidecadal time scales.

links.mechanism: The Nordeste's short rainy season comes when the tropical rain belt reaches its southernmost point, in March and April. With the north Atlantic warm and the south cool, the belt stays north and withdraws early, and sinking air sits over Northeast Brazil instead.
links.caveat: The rains also answer the Pacific: an El Niño dries the Nordeste in the same months through its own arrow, and the two drivers usually arrive together, since an El Niño winter tends to warm the north Atlantic. Southern Bahia can run the other way from the northern Nordeste.
links.evidence_note: The classic mechanism: warm water north and cool water south of the equator drive a local circulation with rising air near 10°N and sinking air over Northeast Brazil; in dry years the north Atlantic is warmer and the ITCZ displaced north; the Nordeste drought is the local face of a rain deficit across the whole equatorial Atlantic tied to the early withdrawal of the ITCZ toward the warm north.

links.mechanism: With the south Atlantic warm and the north cool, the rain belt pushes further south than usual and lingers over Northeast Brazil, giving the Nordeste a good rainy season or floods.
links.caveat: A good year for the sertão can be a flood year for the coast, and a La Niña in the Pacific adds to the wet tendency on its own; the quantity depends on how far south the belt gets and for how long.
links.evidence_note: In wet years the tropical North Atlantic is cooler and the South Atlantic warmer, with the near-equatorial rain belt displaced south and stronger rising air over the Nordeste; the strong negative event of spring 2009, with the belt shifted south, brought severe flooding to Northeast Brazil.

links.mechanism: When the north Atlantic is warm and the south cool, the tropical rain belt sits further north in summer over the eastern Atlantic and West Africa, and the monsoon winds carry moist air deeper into the Sahel.
links.caveat: The mode peaks in spring and the Sahel's rains come in July– September; the arrow assumes the contrast lasts into summer, which it does in some years and not others. The Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean also move the Sahel's rains, and the decades-long swings belong to the AMO's arrow rather than this one.
links.evidence_note: Wet Sahel years go with a warm north and a cool south tropical Atlantic and a rain belt displaced north; over the drought decades the north Atlantic cooled, the south warmed and the wind confluence over the eastern Atlantic moved 150–200 km south, most of all in July–August, enough to account for the fall in Sahel rain; the studies work with the sea-temperature pattern rather than the spring mode itself.

links.mechanism: With the north Atlantic cool and the south warm, the rain belt over the eastern Atlantic and West Africa sits further south in summer, and the monsoon's rains fall short of the Sahel.
links.caveat: Same limits as the wet side: the spring contrast has to last into summer, and the Sahel answers other oceans too. The long drought of the 1970s and 1980s was the AMO's cool decades, not a run of single springs.
links.evidence_note: Dry Sahel years go with a cool north and a warm south tropical Atlantic and a rain belt displaced south; the drought decades show the same pattern in every season, strongest in boreal summer.

links.mechanism: A warm tropical North Atlantic keeps the rain belt and the rising air north of the equator through the southern winter. The trade winds that would carry Atlantic moisture into the southern Amazon weaken, the air over the region sinks, and the dry season runs long and hot.
links.caveat: Known from two droughts, 2005 and 2010, and a short record of correlations, so shown as probable. El Niño dries the Amazon too, but in the wet season and on the northern side of the basin, which is why the map keeps the two regions apart. How much the drought costs depends on the fires people set.
links.evidence_note: The 2005 drought of southwestern Amazonia was not related to El Niño but to the anomalously warm tropical North Atlantic, weaker trade-wind moisture transport into southern Amazonia and weakened rising motion, intensified through the dry season into September; the Atlantic influence over 1979–2005 is comparable to the Pacific's and falls in the dry season; the 2010 drought was intensified by the same warming of the tropical North Atlantic through a longer dry season.

links.mechanism: With the tropical North Atlantic cool and the rain belt sitting south, the trade winds are proposed to carry more moisture into the southern Amazon, so the dry season is milder and the rivers stay higher.
links.caveat: The wet side is an inference from the correlation and the mechanism: the studies are about the two droughts, and there is no well-studied case of a cool north Atlantic spring giving the southern Amazon a gentle dry season. Shown as contested for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The analysis of 1979–2005 finds a linear Atlantic influence on Amazon dry-season rainfall, which would run both ways, but the papers document the dry years only.

links.mechanism: A warm tropical North Atlantic and Caribbean gives the tropical waves that cross it in early summer more moisture and energy, so the first half of the rainy season, from May to July, tends to be wetter over the Caribbean and Central America.
links.caveat: The early season answers the Atlantic; the late season, from August, answers the Pacific, and an El Niño can cancel the wet tendency. The studies use the north Atlantic's temperature rather than the spring mode itself, and the rain belt's position matters more for the Pacific coast of Central America than for the islands.
links.evidence_note: Early-season (May–July) Caribbean rainfall is strongly influenced by warm water in the tropical North Atlantic between the equator and 20°N, the band where tropical waves develop, while the late season answers the equatorial Pacific and Atlantic; Central America is wettest when the north Atlantic is warm and the eastern Pacific cool.

links.mechanism: An El Niño winter weakens the northeast trade winds over the tropical Atlantic through the same chain of high and low pressure that reaches North America. Weaker trades mean less evaporation and less cooling, so the northern tropical Atlantic warms in late winter and the contrast with the south peaks the following spring.
links.caveat: The warming trails the El Niño's peak by four to five months, so from a June start it arrives the following March and most of the mode's own effects fall after the year shown. Not every El Niño warms the Atlantic; a positive NAO winter can undo it.
links.evidence_note: Half to four fifths of the north Atlantic trade-wind belt's temperature variability goes with the Pacific ENSO, with Atlantic warmings four to five months after the mature phase of Pacific warm events, through reduced trade winds and reduced evaporative cooling, best developed in the spring after; almost all extreme north tropical Atlantic springs since 1950 relate to ENSO or the NAO; the mode's spring predictability comes from the tropical Pacific.

links.mechanism: A La Niña winter strengthens the northeast trades over the tropical Atlantic, more evaporation cools the northern side, and the contrast tips the other way the following spring.
links.caveat: The Atlantic's answer to a La Niña is weaker and less regular than its answer to an El Niño, and the study that found the lag looked at warm events; shown one tier lower for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The remote-forcing study finds that the north tropical Atlantic's extreme springs of both signs relate to ENSO or the NAO through the trade winds and evaporation; the lag analysis itself was done on Pacific warm events.

links.mechanism: A negative NAO winter weakens the Azores high and with it the northeast trade winds. Weaker trades evaporate less water from the northern tropical Atlantic, which warms through late winter, and wind and evaporation then feed on each other to hold the warm north through spring.
links.caveat: The NAO changes from month to month, so a single stormy December may not be enough; it is a winter's average that matters. The link is drawn from the NAO as chosen in December; the mode's own summer effects then fall inside the year shown, which is the point of the chain.
links.evidence_note: Almost all extreme north tropical Atlantic springs since 1950 relate to either ENSO or the NAO, which lead them, through changes in surface winds and evaporation; the spring meridional modes are forced by trade-wind variations in the northern subtropical ocean; the 2009 negative event began with a stronger subtropical high and stronger trades in January–February, the mirror case.

links.mechanism: A positive NAO winter strengthens the Azores high and the northeast trades, more evaporation cools the northern tropical Atlantic, and the contrast tips negative in spring, with the rain belt held south.
links.caveat: Same limits as the mirror link: a winter's average matters, not one month, and an El Niño in the same winter works the other way.
links.evidence_note: The strong negative event of 2009 was initiated by stronger than normal trade winds in January and February with a strengthened subtropical North Atlantic high, cooling the ocean by evaporation and deepening the mixed layer; the remote-forcing study ties such springs to the NAO and ENSO.

links.mechanism: Warm water off Baja California weakens the trade winds to its south, the weaker wind evaporates less and warms the sea further, and the warm patch and the weak wind creep south-west together through spring. By summer the weak wind reaches the equator, where it lets warm water spread east and starts the Pacific toward an El Niño by the following winter.
links.caveat: A nudge, not a trigger: the Pacific has to be primed, with heat already stored in the west, for the spring signal to grow, and about one positive spring in three comes to nothing. The spring of 2014 was one such miss. Part of the mode is also El Niño's own footprint in the subtropics, so the two are not fully separate things.
links.evidence_note: The majority of El Niño events over four decades were preceded by the mode's spring warming and south-westerly wind; in a high-resolution coupled model it acts as a trigger seven to nine months before large El Niños, but not every event triggers one and the western Pacific has to be preconditioned; imposing the winter forcing in a coupled model warmed the ENSO region in about 70% of sixty runs; positive springs forecast eastern Pacific El Niños with some skill in a multi-model hindcast; the spring-to-winter relation has strengthened over the past seventy years.

links.mechanism: Cool water off Baja California and stronger trades are proposed to work the mirror way: the stronger wind cools the sea further, the pattern creeps toward the equator, and by summer the stronger easterlies there lift cool water in the east and start the Pacific toward a La Niña.
links.caveat: The negative side is the weak side. In the observed record negative springs are poor predictors of La Niña, and the studies that made the case for the mode are about the positive springs before El Niños. Shown as contested for that reason; the map draws it so the asymmetry can be seen, not because it is reliable.
links.evidence_note: In the multi-model hindcast negative mode events poorly predict La Niña events in observations, and the forecast models fail to capture even that; the subtropical route into ENSO produces multi-year La Niñas but not multi-year El Niños, one source of the asymmetry between the two.

links.mechanism: Rain rising over the warm water of the mode's north-western arm sets up a wave-like response to its west: low-level westerly winds and a spin over the south-eastern part of the typhoon breeding grounds, and weaker wind shear aloft. Typhoons form further east and have a longer run over warm water to grow.
links.caveat: The count is a tendency, not a forecast, and one study finds the year-to-year part of the relation weak once the slow decadal swing of the tropical Pacific is removed; the model experiments that back the link are what keep it at probable. Its effect adds to El Niño's own, which points the same way.
links.evidence_note: A positive mode favours typhoon formation in the western North Pacific and a negative one inhibits it, in observations, a thousand-year control run and sensitivity experiments, through the wind shear over the south-eastern breeding grounds; the mode index correlates with the number of intense typhoons in June–November; the summer of 2018, with no El Niño, had eighteen typhoons and sensitivity runs put the positive mode as the main cause; in 2015 the mode's warm water pushed the mean birthplace of typhoons ten degrees east of 1997's. One study finds the statistical link is dominated by decadal covariation with the tropical Pacific.

links.mechanism: With the subtropical north-east Pacific cool, the wave-like response over the typhoon grounds runs the other way: stronger wind shear and less spin over the south-eastern breeding grounds, so typhoons form closer to Asia and stay weaker.
links.caveat: The composite study finds the quiet tendency, but the case studies and the model experiments are about positive springs, and the objection that the year-to-year relation is weak applies with more force here. Shown one tier lower than the warm side for that reason.
links.evidence_note: The negative phase inhibits typhoon occurrence in the western North Pacific in the composite analysis of observations and the control run; the one-in-ten-years component of the relation, rather than the year-to-year one, carries most of the signal.

links.mechanism: The mode's warm water lies over the western part of the eastern Pacific hurricane grounds, between Mexico and Hawaii. Warm sea, moist air and weak wind shear there give storms more fuel and more room, and more of them travel west toward Hawaii.
links.caveat: Rests on one season, 2015, and its model experiments, and that season had a strong El Niño at the same time; the record of storms in this basin is short. Shown as contested until more seasons are studied.
links.evidence_note: The record 2015 season in the eastern and central Pacific, with the first three simultaneous category-4 hurricanes and a record count around Hawaii, was not primarily caused by the El Niño but by warm water in the subtropical Pacific typical of the positive mode, according to targeted high-resolution experiments; the western part of the basin set records for storms, hurricane days and storm energy in 2015, with the El Niño and the positive mode together giving a record-warm background.

links.mechanism: The haze of sulphuric-acid droplets in the stratosphere reflects a few per cent of incoming sunlight back to space. Less sunlight reaches the surface, the land and the upper ocean lose more heat than they gain, and the world's average temperature drops by a few tenths of a degree, most in the first summer after the eruption, then creeps back over two or three years as the haze settles out.
links.caveat: The dip is small next to a strong El Niño or the warming trend, and is easiest to see once El Niño's own warmth is taken out of the record. The map cannot weigh a cooling volcano against a warming El Niño: when both point at this region it shows a disagreement, as in 1992, when in reality the volcano won and the world cooled despite the El Niño.
links.evidence_note: A climate-model forecast made within months of Pinatubo predicted cooling from late 1991 peaking in late 1992, large enough to overwhelm the developing El Niño's warmth; observed global temperatures fell by up to half a degree by mid-1992, and satellite lower-troposphere temperatures by half a degree by September 1992; a composite of five major tropical eruptions shows significant cooling once ENSO is removed; ten reanalyses agree on tropical cooling after most but not all eruptions; the observed drying of the air amplified the cooling, which a model could not reproduce without water-vapour feedback.

links.mechanism: A cooler surface evaporates less, so there is less water in the air to rain out, and the land cools faster than the sea, which weakens the contrast that draws the summer monsoon inland. If the haze sits more in the northern hemisphere, as most tropical clouds do, the tropical rain belt also shifts south, away from the Sahel.
links.caveat: Comes mostly from models and a handful of twentieth-century eruptions; in the observed record the summer signal is only marginally detectable, and the sign depends on which hemisphere gets more haze: a cloud that stays south of the equator can leave the Sahel wetter. The high-latitude eruptions that dried the Sahel most, Laki in 1783 among them, are not on this map. For a June eruption the next Sahel rains fall in the month after the year shown, so the arrow stays waiting.
links.evidence_note: Global and monsoon rainfall drop after eruptions in CMIP5 models and in three observational datasets, with the rain belt shifting away from the hemisphere holding more aerosol; land precipitation and river runoff fell to record lows in the year after Pinatubo once ENSO is accounted for; a hemispherically lopsided haze shifts Sahelian rainfall, with northern-hemisphere loading drying the Sahel in a model and in the record; most CMIP5 models show clear reductions of summer monsoon rainfall in the first year after large eruptions since 1850; the warm-season influence is only marginally detectable in the observations; a model of the 1783 Laki eruption dried the Sahel by one to three millimetres a day and cut the flow of the Nile.

links.mechanism: The monsoon is driven by the summer contrast between hot land and cooler sea. Under the haze the land cools faster than the ocean, the contrast weakens, and a cooler atmosphere holds less water, so the first monsoon after the haze has spread tends to bring less rain.
links.caveat: Most of the evidence is from models. The tree-ring record of monsoon Asia shows drier central Asia but wetter mainland south-east Asia in eruption years, which the models do not reproduce, and India's own monsoon of 1992 was only modestly below normal. Both the eruption and any El Niño it may favour point the same way, so the two are hard to separate in the record.
links.evidence_note: Monsoon rainfall decreases after eruptions in CMIP5 models and in observations; most CMIP5 models show clear reductions of summer monsoon rainfall in the first year after large eruptions; in a last-millennium ensemble northern-hemisphere cooling shifts the rain belt toward the equator and suppresses the south-east Asian monsoon even without an El Niño; drought reconstructions find drier central Asia but wetter mainland south-east Asia in eruption years, so models may miss part of the response; large eruptions strengthen the coupling between ENSO and the Indian monsoon in a model and in a millennium of records; land rainfall and runoff fell to record lows in the year after Pinatubo.

links.mechanism: The haze absorbs some sunlight and warms the stratosphere over the tropics more than over the pole. The sharper contrast strengthens the winter polar vortex, the jet beneath it shifts north, and mild Atlantic air is carried deep into northern Europe in the first winter after the eruption, outweighing the cooling from lost sunlight. This is the "winter warming" of a cool volcanic year.
links.caveat: The observed pattern is an average over a dozen eruptions and a single winter can go either way; models produce it weakly if at all, and one study argues the mild winter of 1991–92 after Pinatubo was probably chance, or the El Niño's doing, rather than the volcano's. Second winters show little of it, and the map's season gate cannot tell a first winter from a second.
links.evidence_note: The twelve largest eruptions of 1883–1992 were followed by winter warming over Eurasia and North America significant at the 95% level, in the first winter for tropical eruptions; the same pattern follows fifteen tropical eruptions in half a millennium of European reconstructions, with a positive NAO; four centuries of records give a mean response resembling the Arctic Oscillation but a spread larger than the mean; the winter warming after Pinatubo is reproduced in one model and much more weakly than observed or not at all in the IPCC AR4 and CMIP5 ensembles, though most CMIP5 models show it when only the first winter is examined; large ensembles find the effect tiny next to winter-to-winter variability, and the 1991–92 warming is reproduced in one model only with the observed El Niño sea-surface temperatures specified; all datasets in a ten-reanalysis comparison show the warm anomaly over northern Europe.

links.mechanism: The same strengthened winter vortex and stronger westerlies that warm northern Europe reach furthest east over Russia and Siberia, the core of the winter-warming pattern, where the first winter after a tropical eruption tends to be milder than usual even while the planet as a whole is cooler.
links.caveat: The same evidence as for northern Europe, with the same doubts: a tendency averaged over a dozen eruptions, weak in most models, and possibly chance in the one winter, 1991–92, that everyone remembers. The map cannot tell a first winter from a second, and the second shows little of it.
links.evidence_note: Warming over Eurasia after the twelve largest eruptions since 1883, in the first winter after tropical ones; warm anomalies throughout northern Eurasia in four centuries of cold-season reconstructions and in model simulations of them; observed January circulation changes after three eruptions explained by stationary-wave changes under a strengthened polar-night jet; CMIP5 models fail to capture the Eurasian warming when two winters are combined but most show it in the first winter alone; the effect is tiny against internal variability in large ensembles.

links.mechanism: Heating of the tropical stratosphere by the haze strengthens the winter polar vortex, and a strong vortex reaches down to the surface as a positive North Atlantic Oscillation: the Iceland low deeper, the Azores high stronger, the westerlies across the Atlantic stronger and further north.
links.caveat: Found in the pressure record after most large eruptions but, in the words of one review of ten reanalyses, not as clear cut as the literature suggests: the spread between eruptions is large, models make the vortex response small, and the polar response turns out not to be a direct effect of the heating but to go through stratospheric wave activity, sensitive to the shape of the cloud.
