Drawn dashed for that reason; with the chain on, the NAO's own winter arrows follow one tier down.
links.evidence_note: Both the Arctic Oscillation and the NAO are excited in the first winter after thirteen major eruptions since 1870, significant at 95%, the signal larger for the NAO; the winter response to fifteen tropical eruptions in European reconstructions follows a positive NAO; four centuries of records give a mean response resembling the Arctic Oscillation; ten reanalyses and the Hadley Centre pressure record confirm a positive NAO tendency in the winters after large eruptions, with a large spread for individual eruptions; AR4 models simulate a positive Arctic Oscillation but with far weaker surface effects, and CMIP5 models generally fail to capture the strengthened vortex and positive NAO; in one Earth-system model the vortex response is insignificant for observation-based forcings and depends on the structure of the aerosol cloud.

links.mechanism: Two routes are proposed. The haze cools land faster than sea, and cooling over tropical Africa weakens the West African monsoon and sends a wave of westerly wind along the equator that reaches the western Pacific and lets warm water spread east. And in the eastern Pacific the cold water welling up from below is cooled less than the surface around it, so the west cools more than the east, the trade winds slacken, and the Pacific drifts toward El Niño in the year after the eruption.
links.caveat: Genuinely unsettled. Coral and tree-ring records and CMIP5 composites lean toward an El Niño in the year after big tropical eruptions, but a thousand years of central-Pacific coral finds no significant response, one model starts with a La Niña before any El Niño, and the answer depends on the season of the eruption and on what the Pacific was already doing: an eruption in a La Niña year does little. Pinatubo's own El Niño was already under way when it erupted, so 1991 cannot settle the question.
links.evidence_note: Proxy records show an El Niño-like response to volcanic forcing over the past several centuries; in an intermediate model only eruptions larger than Pinatubo shift El Niño likelihood above internal variability, and volcanism raises the odds by about half on average rather than triggering events; CMIP5 shows an El Niño tending to peak in the year after large eruptions, with targeted simulations tracing it to cooling over tropical Africa; 122 CMIP5 members show co-occurring El Niño and positive Indian Ocean Dipole events peaking six to twelve months after the forcing peaks; a Pinatubo-size eruption produces a significant El Niño response a year on in one coupled model except when the Pacific starts in La Niña, and more strongly for summer eruptions; another coupled model gives an El Niño-like warming a year after the peak forcing, and the eruption season matters for the eruption-year response; against it, fossil corals from the central Pacific show only a weak, insignificant El Niño-like tendency over the last millennium, and one coupled model's first response is La Niña-like.

stories.title: The 1997–98 El Niño
stories.intro: The strongest El Niño of the twentieth century. Follow it month by month and compare what the map expects with what actually happened, including the places where the real event broke the pattern.

steps.text: In spring 1997 the trade winds along the equator weakened and warm water spread east across the Pacific. By May the sea surface off Peru was already far warmer than normal, and by the end of the year the warming was the largest ever measured. Everything that follows on this map starts from this one change.

With the warm water and the rising air moved east, Indonesia sat under sinking, dry air. The rains failed across much of the region. Fires lit to clear land burned out of control in the dried-out peat and forest, and smoke haze covered Southeast Asia for months.

Strong winds high over the Atlantic, set up by El Niño, tore developing storms apart. The 1997 Atlantic hurricane season was well below average, with fewer storms than usual and not a single named storm during August, normally the start of the peak season.

Here the pattern broke. A strong El Niño usually means a weak Indian monsoon, and 1997 was expected to bring drought. Instead, monsoon rain over India came in close to normal. Scientists have offered several explanations, including where in the Pacific the warmest water sat. The map shows the tendency, not what happened this time.

Eastern Australia was drier than usual through the second half of 1997, as expected, though the drought was less severe than in the big El Niño of 1982–83. Australian forecasters point to 1997 as a reminder that a strong event in the Pacific does not guarantee a strong effect on land.

In East Africa the effect ran the other way. Warm water also spread across the western Indian Ocean, and the October–December "short rains" turned into months of extreme rainfall. Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia saw some of the worst flooding on record, with roads and villages washed away.

December 1997 was the peak. Heat stored in the tropical Pacific was being released to the atmosphere, and with it the whole planet warmed. 1998 became the warmest year in the instrumental record at the time: an El Niño spike on top of the long-term warming trend.

Off Peru the warm water sat like a lid on the ocean, shutting off the cold, nutrient-rich water that normally rises from below. Plankton dwindled, the anchoveta moved away or died, and the catch collapsed, as it had in the 1982–83 event.

The normally bone-dry coast of Peru and Ecuador had a summer of torrential rain. Rivers that are usually dry flooded, mudslides cut the Pan-American Highway, and thousands of homes were destroyed. This is one of the most reliable El Niño effects, and 1997–98 was among the wettest cases.

California's link to El Niño is marked as contested on this map, because in many events little happens. 1997–98 was the exception that made the link famous: a string of winter storms brought heavy rain, floods and coastal damage. Studies since then suggest the effect is real mainly in the strongest events.

Months of unusually warm water pushed corals past their limit. 1998 saw the first mass coral bleaching recorded across the whole tropics, with severe reef death in the Indian Ocean and parts of the Pacific.

By May 1998 the warm water was gone, and the Pacific swung quickly into a La Niña that lasted into 2000. The twelve months of this map are a snapshot of the classic El Niño year; the return swing is the next story.

stories.title: A La Niña year in the Southern Hemisphere
stories.intro: La Niña is the cool sister of El Niño, and many of its effects are the mirror image. This walkthrough follows a typical La Niña year south of the equator, where the effects are among the strongest, and stops at the places where the mirror does not quite hold.

steps.text: The trade winds strengthen, piling warm water up in the far western Pacific and drawing cold, deep water to the surface off South America. Rising air and rain concentrate over Indonesia and northern Australia. Notice that some places with a solid El Niño arrow get a dashed La Niña arrow: the science is less symmetric than the names suggest.
With the warm pool close by, Indonesia and the Maritime Continent get more rain than usual from the very start of the event. Flooding is the typical hazard, the opposite of the El Niño fire season.

Eastern Australia is the textbook La Niña region: wetter winters and springs, more tropical cyclones, higher flood risk. The 2010–11 La Niña brought one of the wettest springs on record and widespread flooding in Queensland, including the city of Brisbane.

On the other side of the Pacific, central Chile tends to have a dry winter. The storm track that would bring rain to Santiago stays further south. The link is rated probable: it shows up in most, not all, La Niña winters.

Near the equator in East Africa the October–December "short rains" tend to fail. The 2010–11 La Niña coincided with severe drought in Somalia and northern Kenya, though that drought had other causes as well. The map shows one contributing tendency, not the whole explanation.

Spring in Uruguay, southern Brazil and the Argentine pampas tends to be drier during La Niña, the reverse of the El Niño floods. Farmers in the region watch the Pacific closely for exactly this reason.

The summer rainy season over South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique tends to be wetter than normal, sometimes with damaging floods. The effect is rated probable: the Indian Ocean has a say too, and the relationship has not held in every event.

The coast of Peru and Ecuador stays cool and dry, its usual state made a little stronger. Where El Niño brought floods, La Niña brings nothing unusual to the desert, which is why this link is drawn as probable rather than established: the change is subtle.

Offshore, the stronger upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water feeds one of the richest fisheries on Earth. Anchoveta catches tend to be good in La Niña years, though fishing quotas and the stock's own history matter as much as the ocean does.
The rainy season in Northeast Brazil, February to May, tends to be wetter. This is one of the longest-lagged links on the map: the effect arrives most of a year after the Pacific first cooled.

With the Pacific storing heat rather than releasing it, the whole planet runs slightly cooler for a year or so. The strong 2010–11 La Niña was even measurable in sea level: so much rain fell on land, especially in Australia, that global sea level briefly dropped.

La Niña events often last longer than El Niño and frequently return for a second year, so the twelve months shown here can repeat. Markers that stay hollow in this scenario have no La Niña link in the literature collected here. That is a real gap, not an oversight.

stories.title: The 2019 positive Indian Ocean Dipole
stories.intro: One of the strongest Indian Ocean Dipole events on record, and a rare one: the Pacific stayed close to neutral, so this year shows the Indian Ocean acting largely on its own. Follow it from the dry season in Indonesia to floods in East Africa and the run-up to Australia's Black Summer fires.

steps.text: By June 2019 the sea off Sumatra was cooling while the western Indian Ocean warmed, and the difference between the two kept growing until October, when it reached the largest value since 1997. With El Niño absent, forecasters watched the Indian Ocean as the main driver of the second half of the year.

With cool water off Sumatra, the dry season deepened and dragged on. Fires lit to clear land spread through peat and forest in Sumatra and Borneo through August and September, and haze closed schools and airports in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. It was the worst fire season since the El Niño year of 2015.

The link to the Indian summer monsoon is marked contested, and 2019 shows why it is on the map at all. After a slow start the monsoon finished well above normal, with an unusually wet September. The Indian Ocean is one of several explanations offered; the map shows a tendency that the science has not settled.

Across southern Australia the winter rains fell short, and spring was drier still. The Murray–Darling basin was already deep in a multi-year drought, and forests from Queensland to Victoria dried out. This is the textbook positive-dipole footprint, and 2019 was among the clearest cases on record.

In East Africa the short rains arrived early and heavy. From October to December floods and landslides struck Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan, displacing hundreds of thousands of people. The unusually wet ground then let desert locusts breed in numbers not seen for decades.

Southern India and Sri Lanka had a wet end to the year, in line with the map's tendency for the northeast monsoon. The link is rated probable: it appears in most strong events but the Pacific also has a say in this season.

In December the monsoon winds reversed and the event collapsed within weeks. The Indian Ocean's own push was over, but the dried landscape it left behind in Australia burned on into January in the Black Summer fires. The map stops where the driver's influence stops; what came next was the legacy of a dry year.

stories.title: The winter of 2009–10: a record negative NAO
stories.intro: The most strongly negative North Atlantic Oscillation winter since records began in the 1820s. Follow it from a frozen Britain to record snow in Washington, floods in southern Spain and a mild Greenland, and see why one winter is never the work of one driver alone: an El Niño was under way in the Pacific at the same time.

steps.text: In December 2009 the pressure difference between Iceland and the Azores collapsed and stayed collapsed. Averaged over December to February it was the lowest in a record going back to 1823. A high pressure "block" parked itself near Greenland and the mild westerlies that normally cross the Atlantic in winter stopped arriving.

Snow fell across Britain, Germany and Poland from mid-December and the cold held on into February. The winter was the coldest in the UK since 1978–79. One study made a point that belongs on this map: given how weak the westerlies were, the winter was actually milder than the same pattern would have produced fifty years earlier. The tendency was textbook; the warming climate changed the baseline it acted on.

With the storm track pushed south, Atlantic depressions ran into Portugal and Spain one after another. December to February was the wettest winter in southern Iberia for decades; the Guadalquivir flooded, and reservoirs that had been low for years filled in a season. This is the wet side of the seesaw that dries Iberia in positive winters.

In February 2010 back-to-back snowstorms buried Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia, breaking seasonal snowfall records. The negative NAO steered the cold air south, but a study of the winter credits the El Niño in the Pacific with supplying the moisture. Two drivers, one snowstorm: the map shows them one at a time, so switch to ENSO and El Niño to see the other half.

While Europe and the eastern United States shivered, west Greenland and the Canadian Arctic had a remarkably mild winter, with temperatures far above normal for the season. That is the Greenland–Europe seesaw noticed two centuries ago, and it is the clearest sign that the whole pattern is one thing, not a set of separate cold snaps.

The pattern stayed negative into March and eased in spring. The following winter, 2010–11, opened with another strongly negative December, and then the index swung positive: this driver keeps no calendar. A run of negative winters says little about the next one, which is why the map calls its timescale "weeks to months".

stories.title: 1997: El Niño sets off the Indian Ocean Dipole
stories.intro: The same El Niño as the first story, seen from the Indian Ocean. Here the map follows a chain: El Niño pushes the Indian Ocean Dipole into its positive phase, and the dipole's own effects then join El Niño's. Turn "Follow links through other drivers" off to see the map without the chain. As before, the places where 1997 broke the pattern are the teaching points.

steps.text: By May 1997 the central and eastern Pacific were warming fast and the trade winds had slackened. On this map that single change is the start of everything else, including, one hop away, a change in the ocean next door.

As the rising air over Indonesia weakened, the winds along the equatorial Indian Ocean swung toward the west and cool water rose off Sumatra. The dipole marker turns orange: the map now treats the Indian Ocean as a second driver, set off by El Niño, and follows its links one confidence step lower. In 1997 the dipole began unusually early and grew into the strongest on record.

Two arrows now reach Indonesia: El Niño's directly, and the dipole's through the chain. Both push the same way, toward drought, and the map keeps the state at "drier". The 1997 dry season was one of the harshest on record and the peat and forest fires that followed covered Southeast Asia in haze for months.

This marker has no El Niño link of its own; it is lit only through the dipole. With the chain switched off it stays hollow. Cool water off Sumatra means less moisture feeding the fronts that bring winter and spring rain to Victoria and South Australia, and the second half of 1997 was dry across much of the southeast.

Two pushes in the same direction again. El Niño and the warm western Indian Ocean both feed the October to December short rains, and in 1997 they came as floods: the heaviest rain in decades across Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia, with rivers over their banks from October into early 1998.

November 1997 was the dipole's peak. On the map its link from El Niño runs only from June to November, because the dipole cannot survive the reversal of the monsoon winds in December; step one month on and the dipole drops back to grey while El Niño carries on. Real events do end this way: the 1997 dipole collapsed in December.

Here the chain broke. In a moderate El Niño winter the map expects the Atlantic pressure pattern to lean negative from January, with a cold northern Europe behind it. The winter of 1997-98 did not oblige: the pattern stayed positive and Europe was mild. Studies since suggest that the very strongest El Niños disturb the atmosphere in a different way from moderate ones, which is why the link is drawn dashed and rated only probable.

By May 1998 the warm water was gone and the Pacific tipped into a La Niña that lasted into 2000. On this map La Niña has its own link to the dipole, pushing it negative, and 1998 did bring a negative dipole. Whether the dipole in turn helps set up the next El Niño is the contested feedback listed on the ENSO card; it is told in words, not drawn, because the map never lets an effect loop back onto the driver you chose.

stories.title: 2010–11: La Niña and a negative dipole together
stories.intro: The first story with two drivers chosen by hand. In 2010 a strong La Niña coincided with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole, and the two pushed many of the same places the same way. Here the dipole is not set off by a link from La Niña; you choose both phases, both hold all year, and the map adds their effects up. Where two chosen drivers push a place opposite ways the marker turns hatched and its card says "conflicting"; try swapping the dipole to positive to see that.

steps.text: By June 2010 the El Niño of the previous winter had collapsed and the Pacific was swinging into La Niña, which by the end of the year was among the strongest on record. Two driver markers are lit from the start: La Niña here, and a negative dipole in the Indian Ocean, both chosen by hand rather than one set off by the other.

The dipole marker is green with a plain white ring, not the dashed ring of a driver pushed by a link. Its links fire at full confidence and its phase holds for the whole year. La Niña's own link into the dipole is not drawn: a chosen driver is never pushed, because you have already decided its phase. In 2010 the water off Sumatra ran warm from winter into spring, the reverse of 1997.

This marker has no La Niña link of its own, so it shows what the second driver adds: a warm eastern Indian Ocean feeds moisture into the fronts that cross Victoria and South Australia in winter and spring. Spring 2010 was Australia's wettest on record, and the southeast's long drought ended in mud.

Two arrows, both pointing the same way. La Niña and a negative dipole each tend to weaken the October to December short rains, and the map keeps the state at "drier" without a conflict flag. The 2010 short rains largely failed across Somalia, Kenya and Ethiopia; when the long rains of 2011 failed too, famine followed in southern Somalia.

Only La Niña's arrow reaches Queensland and New South Wales: the dipole's link runs to the southeast and is out of season by January. That one arrow was enough. Repeated heavy rain from November onward filled the catchments, and in January 2011 floods reached Brisbane and much of southern Queensland.

The dipole marker is still green because the map holds a chosen phase for all twelve months. Real dipoles do not: the 2010 event faded in early summer as the monsoon winds reversed, and by now every dipole arrow is drawn faint, out of season. Choosing two phases is a teaching convenience, not a claim that both patterns lasted a year.

La Niña weakened through autumn 2011 and the Pacific was back to neutral by June, before a second, weaker La Niña formed late in the year. So much rain fell on land in 2010 and 2011 that global sea level dropped for a while; the study that found this called the event "so strong, the oceans fell".

stories.title: 2016: a negative dipole first, then a weak La Niña
stories.intro: The first story where the second driver comes first. In 2016 a negative Indian Ocean Dipole formed in May, months before the Pacific cooled into a weak La Niña in the spring. The year shown begins in September with La Niña; the dipole is set to begin "before the first driver", so it is already in its phase at month 0 and its lags are counted from May. Watch East Africa: the dipole's arrow arrives before La Niña's, because its clock started earlier.

steps.text: Green from the very first frame. The dipole developed from May 2016, matured in July to September and was the strongest negative event in sixty years of records: warm water off Sumatra, cool water off Africa. On the timeline it is already four months old at month 0; the hollow dot on the season dial marks May as already past, and the first tick carries a small arrow to say the same.

The dipole's link to Victoria and South Australia has no lag, so this marker is wet at month 0 rather than lighting up later in the year. Much of Australia was extremely wet from May 2016 onward, well before the Pacific had cooled: the dipole did this on its own, with La Niña nowhere in sight.

Two arrows, pointing the same way: a warm eastern Indian Ocean and a cooling Pacific both feed rain into Indonesia. In 2016 the dipole's share came first, from May, and the usual dry season largely failed to arrive. La Niña's arrow, counted from September, is here from month 0 as well, because its own lag is zero.

Here is the point of starting the dipole early. Its link to the short rains needs three months, and that clock started in May, so the arrow arrives in October, just as the short rains begin. La Niña's link needs three months too, counted from September, so La Niña's arrow is still missing. Had the dipole begun in September with La Niña, this marker would be hollow now.

The Pacific cooled slowly after the huge 2015–16 El Niño. NOAA's index only reached the La Niña threshold in the September to November season, and the event stayed weak. Lim and Hendon argue the dipole helped it along by strengthening the easterly winds over the Pacific. That same-season push has no link on this map; the map's dipole-to-Pacific link is the contested one about the following year, and it is skipped anyway because you chose La Niña by hand.

Now both arrows are in, pointing the same way, and the marker stays "drier" without a conflict flag. The 2016 short rains failed across Kenya and Somalia and a severe drought followed. An attribution study found that La Niña conditions, and the sea surface temperatures that went with them, made the failure more likely, with no clear sign of a climate-change effect on the rain itself.

Still green, ten months on. A chosen phase holds until the end of the year shown, and this one started before it, so the card counts how long it has been held. The real dipole broke down in late 2016 as the monsoon winds reversed. Every dipole arrow is faint now, out of season; the marker is a teaching convenience, not a claim.

La Niña faded almost as soon as it was declared: the index was back near neutral by early 2017, and by this September the Pacific was neutral again, leaning toward La Niña once more late in the year. The dipole marker has now held one phase for sixteen months, which is why its card warns that real events do not last that long.

stories.title: 2019: a broken polar vortex, a negative SAM and the Black Summer
stories.intro: In late August 2019 the stratospheric polar vortex over Antarctica weakened suddenly, something seen only once before, in 2002. Through October the effect worked its way down to the surface and swung the Southern Annular Mode to its most negative on record. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole had already been drying Australia since the winter. The year shown begins in November 2019 with the mode negative; the dipole is set to begin "before the first driver", in June. Watch eastern Australia, where the two arrows point the same way.

steps.text: Between late August and mid-September 2019 the westerly jet high in the stratosphere over Antarctica slowed abruptly and the polar stratosphere warmed by a record amount. From mid-October to December the weakened winds reached the surface and pushed the mode to a record negative: high pressure over Antarctica, the westerly belt loosened and spread north. Forecast systems had seen it coming from late July. The map holds the negative phase for a year; the real swing lasted about three months.

Already in phase from the first frame, and five months old. The dipole grew from June 2019 into one of the strongest positive events on record and dried the winter and spring across most of Australia before the mode swung. Its lags are counted from June, so nothing of it is still waiting when the year shown begins.

Two arrows, the same way. The dipole's dry arrow is here from the winter; the negative mode's summer link starts in November and adds hot, dry northwesterly winds crossing New South Wales and southern Queensland. November 2019 brought record heat and dryness to subtropical eastern Australia, and severe fires burned through the late spring. The ENSO marker is grey: there was no El Niño that year, which is the point of this story.

Dry from the dipole alone. The mode's own link to Victoria and South Australia is the winter one, and in November it is out of season, so the marker shows one arrow, not two. Both arrows leave in December: the dipole's season ends, and the real dipole collapsed then as well, when the monsoon winds reversed.

The map still shows eastern Australia dry from the mode; the dipole's arrow has gone. The fires peaked around the New Year. In reality the mode had already let go: the record negative phase ran from mid-October to December. From here on the map and the season part ways. That is the gap between a tendency held for a year and a swing that lasted three months; the mode's card says so.

A postscript. The dipole's contested link to the following year counts eleven months from June 2019, so in May 2020 the map nudges the Pacific toward La Niña, drawn dotted and one tier down. A La Niña did form in the second half of 2020. Whether the dipole helped it along, or the Pacific was heading there anyway, is exactly what the dotted line is for.

stories.title: 2014–15: the North Pacific flips warm
stories.intro: After a mostly cool decade, the Pacific Decadal Oscillation swung positive in 2014. A huge patch of warm water, nicknamed "the Blob", had built up in the northeast Pacific the winter before and spread to the coast, and by late 2014 the whole basin wore the warm-phase pattern. The year shown begins in November 2014 with the oscillation positive; El Niño is set to begin in March 2015, when it did. Watch the Pacific Northwest, and watch the Southwest for the place where the map's tendency and the real winter parted ways.

steps.text: In the winter of 2013–14 a strong, stubborn ridge of high pressure sat over the northeast Pacific. Under it the ocean lost less heat than usual and the water warmed by the largest amount seen there since at least the 1980s. The warm patch spread to the coast in spring and summer 2014, and NOAA's index for the oscillation turned positive and stayed there. The map holds the phase for a year; the real one lasted several.

The map expects a mild, dry winter in the Northwest, and the winter of 2014–15 was mild above all. Near-normal precipitation fell as rain instead of snow, and by spring more than four fifths of the snow-measuring sites in the far west were at record lows. The warm sea surface, not a lack of storms, was the main cause: model experiments put its share at about twice that of human warming.

Here the pattern broke. The dotted line says the Southwest tends to be wetter in a warm phase, and the map paints it wet. The winter of 2014–15 instead kept California in its exceptional 2011–2015 drought: the wet winter the dotted line promises did not reach it. The oscillation's rainfall signals are weak; El Niño does most of the work, and El Niño had not yet arrived.

In March 2015 NOAA declared an El Niño, which grew through the year into one of the three strongest on record. On this map it is a chosen driver, entering its phase four months after the start, so nothing pushes it. Notice that a positive oscillation and an El Niño are the usual pairing, not a coincidence: much of the oscillation is El Niño's footprint in the North Pacific, and the warm water of 2014 had helped set the stage.

A year on, in November 2015, two arrows point at the Southwest the same way, wet: the oscillation's dotted one and El Niño's solid one, whose lag has now run. Where two drivers agree the map simply holds the state, and the card rates the pair by the weaker line. This is the pairing the research singles out: El Niño's winter pattern over North America comes through most reliably when the North Pacific is in its warm phase. Whether the rain delivers is for the record to say; the map only says the odds have lined up.

stories.title: 1995: the Atlantic turns warm
stories.intro: After thirty years in its cool phase the North Atlantic swung warm in 1995, and the swing showed up at once: the busiest hurricane season in decades, the beginning of a partial recovery of the Sahel's rains, and a run of warmer European summers. The year shown begins in June 1995 with the oscillation positive; a weak La Niña is set to begin in September, when it did. Watch the hurricane region in October, where the two drivers point the same way, and read the last step for what the map cannot settle.

steps.text: The whole North Atlantic had run cool since the mid-1960s. In 1995 the basin-wide average crossed back above its long-term mean and stayed there, the third warm phase in the record after those of the late 1800s and the middle of the twentieth century. The map holds the phase for a year; the real one has held for decades. Whether the ocean's slow overturning, pollution haze or the weather's own noise set the swing is argued over, and the driver card says so.

The map paints western Europe warm, on the dashed line of a probable link. The summers of the late 1990s and 2000s in north-west Europe were warmer than those of the decades before, and wetter too, and that shift has been traced in large part to the Atlantic's swing to warm rather than to the weather of any single year. A few tenths of a degree over a decade, felt as more hot summers than cool ones.

The Sahel had lived through the drought of the 1970s and 1980s with the Atlantic cool. From the mid-1990s its rains came back in part, never to the plenty of the 1950s but well above the drought years, and the map's solid line says why: a warm North Atlantic pulls the tropical rain belt north in summer. Models driven by the observed sea temperatures reproduce the drying and the partial return; what set the ocean's phases is a separate argument.

Two arrows point at the hurricane region the same way, active: the warm Atlantic's solid line and La Niña's, which arrived in September. 1995 delivered one of the most active seasons on record, with nineteen named storms, and the six seasons from 1995 to 2000 saw roughly double the activity of the previous twenty-four years, a doubling that the research at the time laid at the door of the warm Atlantic and the weaker wind shear that came with it.

A year on, in June 1996, the phase held, and it went on holding: the active hurricane era peaked in 2004 and 2005. What the map cannot settle is why the Atlantic swings. One camp reads the record as a natural cycle of the ocean's overturning; another finds that pollution haze and volcanic dust explain most of the twentieth-century swings; a third reproduces the pattern without any ocean circulation change at all. The links on this map run from the warm ocean to the weather and hold whichever camp is right; the phase's next turn is the open question.

stories.title: 1984: the Atlantic's own Niño
stories.intro: In early 1984 the trade winds over the equatorial Atlantic slackened and warm water spread east to the Gulf of Guinea, the strongest warm event in the Atlantic's record to that date. It came in the depths of the Sahel drought, with the North Atlantic in its cool phase, and it was followed by a weak La Niña in the Pacific. The year shown begins in May 1984 with the Atlantic Niño in its warm phase; the cool Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation is set as a second driver that began a year earlier, the nearest the map can come to a phase that had held since the 1960s.

steps.text: In most years the eastern equatorial Atlantic cools sharply in May and June as the trade winds push the warm water west. In 1984 the trades weakened in the early months of the year, the cooling failed and the sea off the Gulf of Guinea ran unusually warm through the northern summer. Unusual enough to get its own paper in Nature: the Atlantic's small cousin of El Niño, seen at full size.

The coast from Liberia to Nigeria has its main rains in May–July, and the map's solid line says a warm Gulf of Guinea feeds them. That is the clearest footprint of an Atlantic Niño: wet years on the coast come with a weak or missing cold tongue offshore, and the coast's rains, unlike the Sahel's, follow the sea just offshore rather than the whole tropics.

Two arrows point at the Sahel the same way, dry: the cool North Atlantic's solid line and the Atlantic Niño's dotted one, and the card rates the pair by the weaker line. 1984 was the worst year of the long drought. The dotted line is dotted for a reason: the old see-saw, in which a warm Gulf of Guinea meant a dry Sahel, faded after the 1970s as the Sahel came to follow the Pacific and the Indian Ocean as much as the Atlantic. In 1984 the Atlantic's two patterns and the wider tropics all leaned the same way.

With the chain on, the Atlantic Niño has pushed ENSO toward La Niña from October: rain rising over a warm Atlantic in summer strengthens the trade winds over the central Pacific, and the Pacific answers by winter. A weak La Niña did form in the Pacific in late 1984 and lasted into 1985. The link is dashed, not solid: it shows up in the record only since the late 1960s, and it nudges the Pacific rather than steering it.

A year on, in May 1985, the map still holds the Atlantic Niño in its warm phase. The real event had faded by the autumn of 1984; an Atlantic Niño lasts three to five months, and the map's twelve-month hold is a simplification. Two more cautions travel with this driver. The Pacific's own El Niño barely reaches the Atlantic, so nothing on this map pushes the Atlantic Niño; and the models used for seasonal forecasts still struggle to reproduce it at all.

stories.title: 1998: the Yangtze floods
stories.intro: The great El Niño of 1997–98 peaked in the Pacific in December and had collapsed by May. What it left behind was a tropical Indian Ocean warmed through the winter, at its warmest in February–April 1998 and still warm into the summer. This story follows that warmth: the year shown begins in February 1998 with the basin in its warm phase and the chain on, so the map can show the basin nudging the Pacific toward the La Niña that followed. The El Niño itself is not set as a second driver, because the map would hold it through a summer in which it had already ended.

steps.text: Through the winter of 1997–98 the El Niño's sinking air sat over the Indian Ocean, with clear skies and weak winds, and the whole basin gathered heat. By February 1998 the sea from East Africa to Sumatra was running unusually warm, and it stayed warm long after the Pacific had cooled: the ocean acts like a capacitor, storing the El Niño's signal and releasing it onto Asia the following summer. Most of the arrows from this marker point at that summer.

The dotted arrow to the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal says fewer storms than usual before the monsoon, and dotted means contested. Here is why. On 9 June 1998 a cyclone came ashore at Kandla in Gujarat and killed thousands of people, one of the deadliest Arabian Sea storms on record, in exactly the season and the year the arrow points to quiet. A tendency is not a forecast, the reliable record of these storms is short, and the studies behind this arrow are few; it is the least certain on the map.

In June the summer rain front settled over the Yangtze valley and stayed. The warm Indian Ocean had built a strong high over the western Pacific, and its winds pumped moist air up the valley for weeks. The river rose to its highest since 1954 and the floods of July and August took thousands of lives and drove millions from their homes. The map's solid arrow is this mechanism: the summer after an El Niño, carried into summer by the ocean the El Niño left warm.

With the chain on, the warm basin has pushed ENSO toward La Niña from June: rain rising over a warm Indian Ocean drives an easterly wind over the far western Pacific, which pushes the warm water west and ends the El Niño quickly. In 1998 the Pacific swung from the strongest El Niño on record to La Niña within a few months, and by July it was there. The arrow is dashed: the push works mostly after strong El Niños, and the Pacific has its own reasons for ending one.

Two arrows point at the typhoon grounds and both say quiet: the warm basin's, through the strong high and the sinking air over the Philippine Sea, and the pushed La Niña's own. The 1998 typhoon season was one of the quietest on record over the open western Pacific, even though the sea there was as warm as ever, which is what first led researchers to look for the cause in the Indian Ocean rather than the Pacific.

A year on, in February 1999, the map still holds the basin warm. The real warmth had faded by the autumn of 1998, as it usually does; the map's twelve-month hold is a simplification. Two more cautions travel with this driver. The basin mode is mostly the echo of an El Niño, not an independent force, so choosing it alone is a way of looking at the second half of an El Niño story. And the 1998 flood was not only the weather's doing: the study of the flood also points to the lakes and forests that had once held the water. The map shows the tendency; the damage depends on what people have done on the ground.

stories.title: 2005: the Amazon dries without an El Niño
stories.intro: In the spring of 2005 the tropical Atlantic north of the equator ran unusually warm and the rain belt sat well north of its usual place. There was no El Niño to blame: the weak one of the previous winter had faded, and the studies of what followed find the cause in the Atlantic. The year shown begins in March 2005 with the meridional mode in its positive phase and no second driver, so the map can show what the Atlantic does on its own: the busiest hurricane season on record and a drought that stranded boats on the Amazon's western rivers.

steps.text: By March 2005 the northern tropical Atlantic was warmer than usual and the southern side cooler, and the belt of tropical rain that normally sits near 5°N in spring had moved north over the warm water. This is the mode in its positive phase. It is usually set off by a winter of weak trade winds, from an El Niño or a negative North Atlantic Oscillation, and then wind and evaporation feed on each other to hold the contrast through spring. In 2005 the Pacific was near neutral by spring, so this story leaves ENSO out and lets the Atlantic act alone.

The first arrow is the shortest. The Nordeste's rainy season comes in March and April, when the rain belt reaches its southernmost point; with the north Atlantic warm the belt stays north and withdraws early, and sinking air sits over Northeast Brazil instead. This is the classic mechanism of Nordeste drought, worked out in the early 1980s, and it is one of the most reliable arrows on the map. El Niño dries the Nordeste in the same months through its own arrow, and the two usually arrive together, since an El Niño winter tends to warm the north Atlantic; here the Atlantic is acting by itself.

From June the solid arrow points at the hurricane grounds and says active. The 2005 season was the most active on record: twenty-eight storms, fifteen of them hurricanes, seven of those major, with Katrina among them, and the records for storms, hurricanes and total storm energy all broken. A warm northern tropical Atlantic with the rain belt north gives storms warm water, moist air and weak wind shear, and moves their birthplace out over the open Atlantic where they have room to grow. The same year sat inside a warm AMO decade, which makes such springs more common; had the AMO been chosen too, its arrow would point the same way and the map would rate the region by the weaker of the two.

By September the drought in the southwestern Amazon was one of the most intense in a hundred years. The Solimões and the Madeira fell to record lows, navigation was suspended, villages along the rivers were cut off, and with the air 3–5°C warmer than usual and the dry season stretched long, fires ran through parts of Acre and Rondônia. The mechanism is the arrow's: the warm north Atlantic kept the rain belt and the rising air north, the trade winds carried less moisture into southern Amazonia, and the air over the region sank instead of rising. The arrow is dashed, because this is known from two droughts and a short record of correlations.

Here is the teaching point. Look at ENSO's marker: it is grey, not part of this scenario, and no arrow reaches the Amazon from the Pacific. The usual suspect for an Amazon drought is El Niño, as in 1926, 1983 and 1998, but those droughts fell in the wet season and on the central and eastern side of the basin. The 2005 drought did not touch central or eastern Amazonia; it fell in the dry season, in the southwest, and the studies of it find the cause in the Atlantic, whose influence on Amazon rain over 1979–2005 is comparable to the Pacific's. Five years later, in 2010, the same warm north Atlantic did it again, and worse.

A year on, in March 2006, the map still holds the mode positive. The real contrast had faded by late summer 2005, as it usually does; the rains returned to the Amazon in October and brought floods after February 2006. Two cautions travel with this driver. It overlaps the AMO on the map and in its effects, and the map does not draw the AMO pushing it, because the same tropical warmth would then be counted twice on the hurricanes, the Sahel and the Nordeste. And a drought's cost depends on the ground as much as the sky: the 2005 dry season turned the forest from a store of carbon into a source, and the fires were set by people. The map shows the tendency; the damage is a human story.

stories.title: 2014–15: the spring warning that came true late
stories.intro: In the spring of 2014 the subtropical north-east Pacific ran warm under weak trade winds, the mode's positive pattern, and forecasters spoke of a coming El Niño to rival 1997's. The year shown begins in March 2014 with the mode positive, no second driver and the chain switched on, so the map can do what the mode does: push the Pacific toward El Niño by autumn. In reality the El Niño stalled that summer, barely reached the threshold in winter, and only became the big event a year later. This is the best example in the tool of what a dashed arrow means: a precursor raises the odds; it does not fix the outcome.

steps.text: The winter of 2013–14 left a huge patch of warm water in the north-east Pacific, nicknamed "the Blob", under a stubborn ridge of high pressure and weak winds. By March the mode's index was positive: warm water and slack trade winds off Baja California, the warmth spreading south-west toward the equator. The map now shows the mode's own arrows, dashed, and with the chain on it will push ENSO in the autumn. Read the caveat first: most El Niños are preceded by a spring like this, but a spring like this is not always followed by an El Niño.

From June a dashed arrow points at the typhoon grounds and says active. Rain rising over the mode's warm water sets up a response far to the west: low-level westerlies, more spin and less wind shear over the south-eastern part of the breeding grounds, so typhoons form further east and have longer to grow. The arrow is dashed for a reason the card gives: one study finds the year-to-year part of this relation weak once the slow swing of the tropical Pacific is removed, and it is the model experiments that keep the link at probable. The map shows the tendency for any positive spring; it does not score the 2014 season.

By September the map has pushed ENSO into El Niño: the marker is outlined as pushed, and a dashed arrow from the mode reaches it. This is the whole point of the driver. In the real 2014 the Pacific had looked like early 1997 until April, with bursts of westerly wind and warm water piled up in the west; then the bursts stopped, and in June an exceptionally strong burst of easterly wind blew the other way and stalled the event. By September the warming was weak and the forecasts of a great El Niño had been quietly withdrawn.

By December the pushed El Niño has painted its own map one tier down: Indonesia and eastern Australia dry, the typhoons active, and in the coming months the Gulf Coast, Peru and Hawaii will fill in, every arrow dashed because it comes through a pushed driver. The real winter of 2014–15 was borderline. NOAA's index hovered at the threshold, and no El Niño was declared until March 2015. The mode had raised the odds; the summer's winds had taken them away again.

A year on, in March 2015, NOAA declared the El Niño at last. The easterly burst that stalled it in 2014 had also stopped the Pacific from releasing its stored heat, which gave the 2015 event a head start, and it grew into one of the three strongest on record. The spring of 2015 was itself strongly positive in the mode, and its warm subtropical water helped make that year's eastern Pacific hurricane season the busiest recorded. So the warning came true, a year late. The lesson to carry from this story is the one the dashed line always carries: a precursor raises the odds, and roughly one spring in three, like 2014, comes to nothing.

stories.title: 1991: Pinatubo
stories.intro: On 15 June 1991 Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines produced the largest volcanic eruption in living memory and put about twenty million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. The year shown begins that June with the eruption on. An El Niño was already building in the Pacific and is set as a second driver from September, chosen by hand: the record has one, and the map's own arrow from the volcano to ENSO is contested. Watch the world cool from September, northern Europe turn mild in December while the planet as a whole is cool, and the map argue with itself about the following June's monsoon. Then read the last step for the two further years the map cannot show.

steps.text: After two months of warnings and the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, Pinatubo blew on 15 June 1991, in the middle of a typhoon. Ash fell across Luzon, but what mattered for the world's climate was the sulphur dioxide carried thirty kilometres up, three times what El Chichón had released in 1982. Satellites watched the cloud circle the globe in about three weeks and straddle the equator, which is why its haze spread over both hemispheres. The map shows the volcano's arrows waiting: the haze takes months to spread and thicken, and its effects arrive in order, the cooling first, the winter next, the monsoons last.

By September the haze covered most of the planet and direct sunlight at remote observatories was down by a quarter. The map now shows the world cooling, a solid arrow, the one link of this driver that nobody disputes. Within months of the eruption a climate model had forecast the dip: cooling from late 1991, deepest in late 1992, and large enough to overwhelm the warmth of the El Niño that was developing. That El Niño enters the map this month as the second driver, and from December its own arrow will point at this region the other way, so the marker will show the two disagreeing. The map cannot weigh them; the forecast could, and it was right.

December, and northern Europe and western Russia turn mild on the map while the planet as a whole is cool. This is the winter warming of volcanic years: the haze heats the tropical stratosphere, the polar vortex strengthens, and the westerlies carry Atlantic air deep into Eurasia. With the chain on, the map also pushes the North Atlantic Oscillation positive and the NAO's own winter map follows one tier down. The winter of 1991–92 really was mild across northern Eurasia and North America. Read the caveat before you credit the volcano: the pattern is an average over a dozen eruptions, and one careful study concludes that this particular mild winter was probably chance, or the El Niño's doing.

March 1992. The El Niño peaked through the winter, a moderate event by the standards of 1982 or 1997, and the map has held two drivers since September. Notice what it does not draw: no arrow from the volcano to ENSO, because the El Niño is chosen by hand and a chosen driver is never pushed. Pick the volcano alone with the chain on and the dotted arrow appears in December instead. Whether eruptions favour El Niño is one of the open questions on this map: the models and some proxies say yes, a thousand years of Pacific coral says no detectable effect, and 1991 cannot settle it, because this El Niño was already under way when the mountain blew.

June 1992: the map's last month, and the first monsoon month after the haze has spread, so the dashed arrow to the Indian monsoon is applied at last, with the El Niño's own arrow beside it, both saying weaker. If the chain is on the marker is hatched instead: the El Niño has pushed the Indian Ocean into a positive dipole and a warm basin, whose arrows say stronger, and the map cannot weigh four arrows against each other, the same tension the 1997 story shows. In reality India's 1992 monsoon came in modestly below normal, and rainfall over land worldwide, with the rivers it feeds, fell to the lowest in the record between October 1991 and September 1992. The Sahel's rains come a month later, just past the year shown, and its arrow stays waiting. Here the map stops and the real story does not: by mid-1992 the world was about half a degree cooler than before the eruption, 1992 and 1993 were both cool years, and the haze had mostly settled out by 1994. The map holds the eruption on for twelve months as a stand-in for a cloud that fades over two years.
